speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. It arises out of the fact that, according to reports, there are some 5,000 freight cars loaded with wheat at the head of the lakes, causing a glut of wheat at that point, and by reason of lack of transportation-

speechtext: Order.

maintopic: CONGESTION OF FREIGHT CARS AT HEAD OF LAKES
speechtext: I understand, Mr. Speaker. Will the minister indicate what the situation is today in the western provinces with regard to moving this wheat, and whether he expects that the present facilities will enable the wheat to be moved before the new crop is ready?

maintopic: CONGESTION OF FREIGHT CARS AT HEAD OF LAKES
speechtext:
The hon. member was good enough to telephone my office indicating that he was going to ask this question. I have a statement which I should like to give to the house. Before doing so, however, I should like to draw the attention of the house to the fact that the last time I was asked a similar question and made a statement in answer thereto it had to do with the shortage of box cars. Strangely enough, today there are in fact too many box cars, and the difficulty is with reference to the movement of the wheat by lake carriers.
It is over a month ago, as a matter of fact on May 11, that I made a review in the house of the movement of western grain. At that time I indicated that the railways and the lake operators had met in full the requirements set down by the Canadian wheat board. The Vancouver situation had been cleaned up and grain was moving freely from the country elevators to both Vancouver and the lakehead; also the lake operators were doing their share in moving the wheat from Fort William and Port Arthur to lower lake ports in the St. Lawrence. However, in the last two or three weeks.


under pressure by the steel companies, some of the lake operators have diverted their ships from the grain trade to the ore trade to fulfil the requirements of our steel mills.
On June 6 the special committee which I appointed, and whose responsibility it is to see that the requirements of the wheat board are met by our transportation agencies, held a meeting and made a full review of the situation prevailing at that time. Pressure was brought to bear on the lake operators, and an undertaking has been given by them to the committee to divert into the grain trade all the ships necessary to take care of the situation which has developed at the lakehead in recent weeks. This situation, naturally, has been caused by the fact that the railways have maintained the tempo of the car loadings at the country elevators, and there has not been sufficient space in the elevators at the lakehead to unload daily the cars delivered by our two railways. The operators met with the wheat board and the grain brokers at the lakehead on Monday of last week, and have given promise to move 16 million bushels before June 23. The grain committee feels that as an immediate step this should take care of the present unfavourable position at the lakehead.

maintopic: CONGESTION OF FREIGHT CARS AT HEAD OF LAKES

subtopic: CANADA-SWEDEN  INCOME TAX    APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA, APRIL 6, 1951
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to give legal effect in Canada to the agreement between the government of Canada and the royal government of Sweden, for the avoidance of double taxation and the establishment of rules for reciprocal fiscal assistance in the matter of income taxes, which was signed at Ottawa on April 6 last.
This agreement, in line with similar agreements we already have with the United States, the United Kingdom and New Zealand, has as its purpose the avoidance of double taxation in respect of trading profits, dividends, interest, and royalty payments flowing between Sweden and Canada. It systematizes taxes imposed on other types of income, including salaries, pensions and annuities which might be taxable in both countries.
Provision is made for tax credit, and for the exchange of information. Article III provides that one country will only tax the industrial and commercial profits of an enterprise of the other country if it has a permanent establishment in that country.
Article VI provides that the withholding tax on dividends will not exceed 15 per cent, or in the case of wholly owned subsidiaries, 5 per cent. Under article XV each country agrees to grant a tax credit for the tax on the dividends withheld by the country of source, or the exemption of such income from taxation.
Article IX provides that remuneration paid by the government of a country for services rendered to that government in the discharge of governmental functions shall be exempt from tax in the other country. Article X provides that an individual who is a resident of one country performing services for or on behalf of a person resident in that country shall be exempt from tax in the other country if he is present there for a period or periods not exceeding 183 days. This rule does not apply to public entertainers.

Article XV provides that Canada will gel a tax credit for tax paid in Sweden in respecl of income having its source in Sweden. Since Sweden has not adopted the system of tax credits, it agrees to give relief by way of exemption from taxation so as to make the relief reciprocal.
Article XVIII provides for the exchange of information.
As I have indicated, this agreement follows the pattern of the agreements Canada already has with the United States, the United Kingdom and New Zealand.

speechtext: In general they are the same. There may be some differences in small details, but they follow the same general pattern as the agreements we already have. The principles involved are the same; they are, of course, the avoidance of double taxation and the establishment of rules for reciprocal fiscal assistance in the matter of income tax. Then it goes into a little further detail. The agreement, in line with other similar agreements, has as its purpose the avoidance of double taxation in respect of trading profits, dividends, interest and royalty payments flowing between Sweden and Canada. It systematizes the taxes imposed on other types of income, including salaries, pensions, and annuities which might be taxable in both countries. Provision is made for tax credits, and for an exchange of information. I do not know that I can point out in detail just the differences, if there are any, with reference to each of the different types of tax mentioned, but the principles followed are precisely the same with reference to the generality of the agreement.

Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this bill is to approve, and to declare as having the force of law in Canada, the convention between the Canadian government and the French government for the avoidance of double taxation and the prevention of fiscal evasion with respect to succession duties. The convention is set out as a schedule of the bill.
As the committee knows, we now have succession duty conventions with the United States and the United Kingdom. These have been followed as patterns in the negotiations with France. The main purpose of this agreement is to provide for a tax credit and for exchange of information.
Article 5 provides that the country of domicile will allow credit against its duty in respect of property taxed by both countries. This credit is the lesser of either (a) its own tax on such property, or (b) the tax of the other country on the same property. This is similar to the provisions in the agreements between Canada and the United Kingdom and Canada and the United States.
Article 7 provides that the two countries will exchange information so that each will be advised of the death of its domiciled decedents and of the composition of their estates. Furthermore, each country will be advised of the composition of estates of persons domiciled in the other country, who have property situated in the first country. maintopic: CANADA-FRANCE  INCOME TAX    APPROVAL OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT PARIS, MARCH 16, 1951
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this bill is to approve and declare as having the force of law in Canada the convention between the government of Canada and the government of the French republic for the avoidance of double taxation and the prevention of fiscal evasion with respect to taxes on income.

This agreement follows the pattern of the agreements which Canada already has with the United States, the United Kingdom and New Zealand.
I have already indicated in my statement on Bill No. 372 the general purpose of such an agreement. I might, therefore, confine my remarks to referring to the important sections of this particular agreement.
Article 4 provides that an enterprise of one country will be subject to tax in the other country on its industrial and commercial profits to the extent that these are attributable to its permanent establishment in the other country.
Paragraph II of article 7 is of particular interest to Canadian companies which have operated in France through wholly-owned subsidiaries. Under these circumstances, there was a tax imposed by France on the profits of subsidiary companies operating there, and another tax on the dividends distributed by a subsidiary company to its Canadian parent. There was also imposed by the French authorities a tax on the Canadian parent company when the latter declared a dividend, a part of which was considered to be the distribution of profits earned in France by reason of the Canadian company's interest in the French subsidiary. Under paragraph II of article 7, France will no longer collect this third tax, so that a Canadian parent company will not be subject to tax on the dividends it pays by reason of its participation in a subsidiary company in France.
Article 9 provides that the salaries paid by one government to its officials who reside in the other state for the purpose of fulfilling their duties will be exempt from tax in such foreign state.
Article 10 provides that the remuneration of those other than government officials will be taxed in the country in which they are employed, unless such employment is merely temporary.
Article 16 provides for the avoidance of double taxation on the types of income therein described by means of tax credits or exemption from tax.
Article 19 provides for the exchange of information.
As I have already indicated, the agreement follows the pattern that has been set by the previous agreements with the other countries I have already mentioned, and the agreements are substantially the same.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM SHERRIDON TO LYNN LAKE, MAN.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lionel Chevrier (Minisier of Transport) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM SHERRIDON TO LYNN LAKE, MAN.
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 376, respecting the construction of a line of railway by the Canadian National Railway Company from Sherridon to Lynn Lake in the province of Manitoba.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM SHERRIDON TO LYNN LAKE, MAN.
speechtext:
Is it the intention of the
Minister of Transport to make a statement?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM SHERRIDON TO LYNN LAKE, MAN.
speechtext:
On the resolution I dealt
with the reasons for the construction of this line. I need not repeat what I said at that time, but briefly perhaps I should summarize the essential features of this bill. They can be divided into four parts.
First, the Canadian National Railways has agreed, subject to the approval of parliament, to construct a line a distance of 155 miles from Sherridon in the province of Manitoba to Lynn lake in the same province. The cost of the line is to be $14,725,000, $10 million of which is to be financed by the Canadian National Railways and the remainder by the government.

The Canadian National Railways has entered into an agreement with Sherritt Gordon, the main features of which are as follows:	Sherritt Gordon will build the
necessary plant and other buildings required to develop the mine, together with a concentrator capable of concentrating 2,000 tons of ore per day. Sherritt Gordon will also build a refinery at Edmonton for the purpose of taking care of the concentrates of nickel.
After the completion of the line the company will agree to pay Canadian National Railways $350,000 a year for a period of twenty years. Then the mining company agrees to locate its plant upon the line of Canadian National Railways and ship its production and products over the C.N.R. line. On the other hand, Canadian National Railways agrees to build a line which will be ready for operation by November I, 1953. It agrees also to operate it in accordance with the traffic and the needs of the traffic prevailing in the area. The railway further agrees that after it has carried an amount of traffic equivalent to 1,880,000 tons of outgoing traffic it will pay Sherritt Gordon mines $2.25 per ton in excess of the 1,880,000 tons until the sum of $5 million has been paid. Canadian National Railways has an agreement or undertaking from the government that any amount in excess of $10 million will be paid by the government, and that amount is estimated at $4,725,000.
The whole reason for the construction is the mineral development that has been found in the area contiguous to Lynn lake in the province of Manitoba. In 1937 Sherritt Gordon Mines Limited began a large scale program of exploration work in the area of the Pre-Cambrian lavas north of Granville lake in northern Manitoba. The result of this work was discovery of gold made at Lasthope lake in 1938 and the discovery of nickel and copper sulphides in small outcroppings near Lynn lake in 1940. Since that time the exploratory work has been going on, and in fact up until the end of 1950 the exploration and development work of Sherritt Gordon has been going on and there has been established the presence of eleven sulphide bodies containing, above a depth of 1,700 feet, a total of 14 million tons of nickel-copper deposits.
Metallurgical tests have indicated that copper concentrate and a nickel concentrate of a satisfactory grade and recovery can be made by treating the nickel-copper sulphides in a flotation mill. The copper concentrates would be shipped to the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company at Flin Flon, and the
Canadian National Railways nickel concentrates would be treated in the proposed ammonia leaching plant to be constructed at Edmonton, Alberta.
The Sherritt Gordon discoveries became generally known during the winter of 1946-47, and a large number of claims were staked by various companies and interests, both large and small, in that area. At the present time the only known mineralized bodies of significance are on claims held by Sherritt Gordon. During the past four years Sherritt Gordon has established the presence of the nickel-copper ore bodies which I have mentioned, and a shaft has been sunk to a depth of 1,024 feet. Mineralized bodies have been investigated underground, but the development work has now ceased pending the completion of plans for production, namely, the construction of the railroad. These deposits cannot be taken out of that area until the railroad is constructed.
^ I should like to bring to the attention of the house the necessity of speed of construction. It is of the greatest importance. Time is of the essence. Everything must be in readiness by October, 1953, at which time the railway company has undertaken to have its line ready for operation. As a matter of fact, the date is November 1, 1953. That is why there is a need for speed in the construction. As hon. members who come from that area know, the period during which construction work can be carried on is a limited one, a matter of some months, so that the railway company will have to move quickly and expeditiously if this line is to be completed by November 1, 1953.
As I indicated in the earlier discussion on the resolution, when debate is completed on the second reading of the bill I propose to move that it be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines for further study.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM SHERRIDON TO LYNN LAKE, MAN.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of the official opposition believe that this mining development is of great importance, and we support this bill which will provide for the construction of a railroad line by Canadian National Railway Company from Sherridon to Lynn lake in northern Manitoba.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) has given the house something of the interesting story behind this project. Apparently large reserves of nickel and copper and cobalt have been discovered at Lynn lake. Under present conditions these are classed as strategic minerals. The minister stated that the government of Canada is paying direct
4212	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways whatever is required to construct this railroad line over $10 million. During the discussion of the estimates of the Department of Defence Production the minister of that department indicated that this amount was estimated at $4,725,000, and was to be given by way of direct capital assistance from his department on the ground that this is defence production. We do not quarrel with such an expenditure under those conditions.
As hon. members know, Sherritt Gordon Mines Limited has been and is a very enterprising company. The annual report for last year shows that at present metal prices the gross value of the recoverable nickel and copper in the ore reserves at Lynn lake amounts to over $175 million-that is without completing the exploration work. It is hoped that there is a great deal more ore there than the amount already found. The report also indicates that the plan of development is to produce approximately 17 million pounds of refined nickel metal per year, 9 million pounds of copper, 300,000 pounds of cobalt and 70,000 tons of ammonium sulphate fertilizer.
We are also very much interested in the fact that the company has a market available for these products. The report sets out that a contract has been made with the stockpiling agency of the United States government for the sale of a substantial portion of the anticipated nickel, copper and cobalt output for the first five years of production. It also indicates that contracts have been made with four of the large nickel consumers among the United States steel producers covering the balance of the nickel and cobalt output for the same period. Apparently the company does not expect any difficulty in disposing of the ammonium sulphate fertilizer and the balance of the copper production at prevailing prices.
They are planning to spend on this development something over $28 million. That amount is over and above the cost of the railway, as I understand it, so that this is a very substantial development.
We are glad to see that they are going to take the nickel concentrates to the vicinity of Edmonton for refining there by natural gas. In recent years members have heard a great deal of talk in this house about natural gas. Here is a case where a large mining company is taking its product to Alberta because natural gas is available there. So far as I know, this is one of the first cases in which that has been done, and it will mean a great deal for the province of Alberta and of course for the dominion at large.


We believe strongly that northern Canada holds the key to the future greatness of this country. Naturally we are very glad to see the developments in northern Quebec and Labrador, where they are opening iron properties. In northern Ontario, you will remember, Mr. Speaker, the great discoveries in the Cobalt area when we were younger . than we are now, but still in this present century. Then there were the subsequent gold developments which led to a tremendous increase in the wealth of Ontario and of the whole of Canada. Now we have a similar development in northern Manitoba, and also the finding of uranium ore in northern Saskatchewan. I believe that if a young Canadian were asking for advice today he could be very well told to "go north, young man," just as many years ago young Americans were told to go west. Personally I think the future of Canada depends on how rapidly and efficiently we open up the north country.
There is one thing we do not understand about the bill, and that is the form in which it is drawn. There is no mention whatever of the agreement between Canadian National Railway Company and Sherritt Gordon Mines Limited. In fact there is no mention of the company in the bill at all. Nor is there any mention of the Department of Defence Production. We find that the mileage is to be 155, that the cost is to be $14,725,000, and that the average cost per mile is to be $95,000 with the power to spend fifteen per cent over that figure. But a person reading the bill and then listening to the explanation of the Minister of Transport would think that he had the wrong bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM SHERRIDON TO LYNN LAKE, MAN.
speechtext: That he had what?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM SHERRIDON TO LYNN LAKE, MAN.
speechtext:
It may be that the bill is in the proper legal form, but I think the agreement should be mentioned therein and should be made a schedule thereto. Without the agreement between the mining company and Canadian National Railway Company there is no justification for a railway. This is not the ordinary case of the construction of a railway. This is a special case in which a company is involved and is willing to pay several million dollars to Canadian National Railway Company. I believe that there should be some mention of the mining company in the bill, and that the whole agreement should be made a schedule to the bill.
I presume that the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines will be considering the measure within the next day or two, and I urge upon the minister that in the meantime some thought be given to amending the bill in the committee so that the whole picture will appear. It is hard

enough to understand statutes even when they are carefully drawn, but in this particular case one would be like a babe in the woods in trying to find out from the bill what is actually taking place. I repeat that we hope the minister will give some thought to inserting terms in the bill which will make its purpose much clearer than it is at the present time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM SHERRIDON TO LYNN LAKE, MAN.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I merely wish to say that we in northern British Columbia are very enthusiastic about the development that is taking place in northern Manitoba, because we have the same problems in northern British Columbia as they have in northern Manitoba. I think the extension of Canadian National Railways in that region will merely be a pattern which will later be followed in British Columbia. I am sure the minister will agree it is high time that he extended the Northern Alberta Railways westward into the fertile wheat fields, the oil fields, and to that region where there is also coal and lumber. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) has said, these developments are good for the whole of Canada. At Lynn lake you have an industry which will help other industries. The farming industry, for instance, will have a market there. The smelter will produce commercial fertilizer which will be so necessary in that part of Canada. That region is not very far from a fertile farming area, as members from Saskatchewan and Manitoba can tell us.
The country needs population. Of course this is a defence project, but I believe that the feeling in that northern country, where there is fertile land and white settlers, is that extending these railroads is an essential part of our defence program.
I would point out to the minister that we need a railway beyond there, to connect Vancouver with Alaska. This very day, labour trouble on the Pacific coast is tying up all our coastal shipping, so that the great military establishments of Alaska are cut off from both the United States mainland and British Columbia so far as water is concerned. So we are back in the traditional Liberal atmosphere now, with new railways being projected and carried forward into the very richest parts of this continent.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM SHERRIDON TO LYNN LAKE, MAN.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to take up much of the time of the house this morning, but I feel I should say a few words on this bill, because the construction of this railway is a matter of vital interest to a large number of my constituents.
The Sherritt Gordon mine went into operation in 1930, and the mine at Sherridon
Canadian National Railways is now worked out. In the last few years the new mine at Lynn lake has been developed; and the closing down of the old mine and the opening of the new have been beautifully co-ordinated so that it requires only this railway to complete the whole project. The old mine will shut down some time this fall, and the surface mining equipment, including the concentrator, will be dismantled and taken over winter roads 150 odd miles to Lynn lake by caterpillar tractors. A large number of the houses of the town will be transported north in the same way. The concentrator will be set up, and when the railway reaches there in 1953 they will be all ready to transport the concentrates to the new refinery at Edmonton.
On a previous occasion I gave the house some figures to illustrate just what an operation of this kind means to the Canadian economy. The mine at Flin Flon came into operation in 1930 with ore reserves of approximately 19 million tons. Now, twenty-one years later, Flin Flon is a town of 12,000 people, and last year produced $40 million worth of metals. At the present time it still has ore reserves amounting to 19 million tons. In 1949 it paid into the federal treasury in ore royalties and direct taxes some $5,500,000, almost the amount now being paid out of the federal treasury to construct the line to the new operation. In indirect taxes the mine paid in the neighbourhood of a million and a half. In proportion to population these payments in taxes amount to about five times the national average. In the last twenty-one years approximately $450 million worth of metals have been produced at the Flin Flon mines. There is a factor to be added to primary production to reach the gross national product attributable to that production, and that factor has been worked out at approximately two and a half. The minister gave the production from this new development as approximately $14 million a year for the next twenty years, or a total of $280 million. Multiplying that by the factor of two and a half gives you an increase in the gross national product of the Canadian economy in the next twenty years of approximately $700 million.
The amount being paid from the federal treasury for this development is only five-sevenths of one per cent of that $700 million, and those figures do not take into account the value of the ore that may lie beyond the last drillhead. In working out the economics of a proposition such as this you cannot go beyond the last drillhead because there is always the distinct possibility that there is no ore beyond that; but you do not know

Canadian National Railways until the drill has been pushed through. In the case of the Flin Flon mine, as I have shown, we have mined three times the ore that was blocked out at the time the operation started. Therefore it is reasonable to suppose that a considerable amount of ore lies beyond the last drillhead, and that the addition to the gross national product may be three times the figure I have mentioned.
Some hon. members have raised the point that the mine at Lynn lake will be the only source of revenue for this railroad. I would point out that in northern Manitoba we have a very large fresh water fishing industry. Some ninety-five per cent of that fish goes to the United States and brings in United States dollars. Last year in the neighbourhood of six million pounds of fish were taken in northern Manitoba. The greater part of that fish comes in by tractor train over winter roads to the present railhead. This railway will move that frontier back approximately 150 miles, thus benefiting all the fishermen in northern Manitoba.
No doubt hon. members are also aware of a recent article in the New York Times referring to uranium deposits at Black lake in northern Saskatchewan, in which it was mentioned that railway facilities would be required. I would point out that if this railway were eventually extended from Lynn lake to lac du Brochet, around north of Reindeer lake and Wollaston lake, it is the logical line to be extended to the vicinity of Black lake. From there it is only a short jump to lake Athabasca, Hay river and Great Slave lake, and from there it is still only a short jump to the Mackenzie valley and across to the Yukon and Alaska, covering the area just mentioned by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray). Another point in that connection is that this line would run completely through the great Canadian shield, which, as everyone knows, is the greatest source of minerals in the world, and which is the foundation for Canada's greatness in the years ahead.
Therefore I do not look upon this proposed extension as a railway for Lynn lake only. This is really for the development of Canada, and the Lynn lake mine is merely the spark justifying that development economically at the present time. I want to commend the Canadian National Railways for being prepared to undertake this operation, and I would like also to commend the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) for being prepared to recommend this operation to his colleagues and through them to parliament and through parliament to the people of Canada. His faith in our northern country will not be misplaced.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM SHERRIDON TO LYNN LAKE, MAN.
speechtext:
My colleague from Manitoba who preceded me has given a pretty good description of what this railway means to our province. I want to assure him and the minister that we who live in the south are wholeheartedly behind this project. We know the tremendous benefit it will bring to the north, and you cannot benefit the north without benefiting the south at the same time. I have had the pleasure of being up in that northern country, and I know the tremendous amounts of fish caught there. We can do with some good fish in the south, though we have our lakes there also.
As the hon. member has said, this development will establish a new frontier, and will mean a great deal to everyone in our province. I congratulate the minister upon pushing this measure forward, and I am sure it will prove to be of benefit not only to Manitoba but to the whole of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM SHERRIDON TO LYNN LAKE, MAN.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to point out one thing to the minister. I am wholeheartedly in favour of this bill. The reason for the discovery of these nickel properties is that the original prospectors were looking for gold. This is just another example, therefore, of the usefulness of gold to the development of our country. Gold is the magnet which draws prospectors into the north. Gold is the magnet which is responsible for the development of other metals in our country. The original discoveries of the various mines in northern Quebec and around Noranda and Rouyn were the result of the search for gold. Gold has been and still is the main metal of our mining development, and this Lynn lake discovery is merely an example of its power to push back the frontier.
There is another thing that has made the development of this property possible, and that is the tremendously important work being done by Canadian scientists, many of them in the department of mines, with regard to geophysical surveys. Without the geophysical survey method it is doubtful-I believe "doubtful" is the right word- whether this property would have been developed as quickly as it has been. Possibly it might not have been developed at all. The geophysical method established what is known as the anomalies, and showed that there were large deposits of metal or substances heavier than the normal rock. The diamond drills definitely proved these deposits. First you have gold bringing the prospectors. Then you have the scientists, the geophysicists who showed that there was a body of different mineral there. Then you have the mining engineer who proved the property;

then the capitalist and miner who developed the mine. It is all one Canadian team which has done this job.
With regard to the whole railway question, Mr. Speaker, I expect that the profits which will eventually accrue to the Canadian people through the development of our mineral resources in northern Manitoba, Saskatchewan and possibly the Northwest Territories will be a far greater source of revenue to the railways than those obtained from developing the port of Churchill, probably many times more, and in this way will prove the wisdom of constructing the Hudson Bay railway.
It will do one more thing which we must bear in mind. It will show that the western provinces have an enormous potential so far as mining is concerned. We used to think of the three western provinces as being tied to a wheat economy. The disasters which resulted from trying to run that great area on a one-crop economy have in the past brought financial problems and despair. In my opinion, this development of the rocks of the prairies will prove to be of greater value in the next quarter century than the wheat economy for the same period.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
I am in the hands of the house, Mr. Speaker. The bill which will be founded on this resolution puts into statutory form order in council P.C. 741 of February 17, 1950, which authorizes grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes on federal properties under certain circumstances.
The house will recall that for the first year -it may be two years now-we provided the necessary funds by an item in the estimates. But at the time I announced the new policy and the formula upon which these grants would be continued, I said that at the appropriate time a bill would be introduced to provide for permanent legislation for the making of these grants. I had contemplated making a brief statement on the operations of the act when the bill was called for second reading. I thought perhaps the house might like to see the bill, that I would -make a brief statement on second reading and it could be discussed then. But I am quite prepared to make that statement now if the house prefers it. It seemed to me that, at this stage of the session, matters might be expedited if we got the bill before the house. But whatever the house wishes is agreeable to me.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: Let us have it now.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: If it would meet with the convenience of the minister, I think we might have the statement now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
It is quite satisfactory to me. My suggestion was just an endeavour to expedite matters. Perhaps the committee on rules will provide some help in that respect.
As I said, this bill puts into statutory form the provisions of order in council P.C. 741 of February 17, 1950, which authorizes grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes on federal properties under certain circumstances. Hon. members will recall that this -new policy announced by the government in November, 1949, was given parliamentary sanction by means of a vote in the 1950-51 estimates which

was governed by the provisions of the order in council to which I have referred. Both in November 1949 and during the past session I undertook to put this policy into statutory form during this session of parliament.
The policy of making grants in lieu of taxes to those municipalities in which there are abnormal concentrations of federal property has been a new venture, and, as in all new ventures, there have been some delays and a few misunderstandings during the first year of its application. I am satisfied, however, that this first year of practical experience has shown that the general principles and policies laid down have worked well and have given a large measure of satisfaction to the municipalities concerned.
The grants authorized by the bill are related to federal properties considered necessary for the functioning of government, but not including properties administered by crown corporations, commissions, boards or agencies established to perform special functions, such as the national railways, the national harbours board, Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and the like. These companies, commissions, boards or agencies have been instructed to negotiate arrangements with municipalities for allowances in lieu of taxes that are fair and equitable having regard to all relevant crcumstances.
The grants provided by this bill are of three kinds: ordinary grants in lieu of general and school taxes; grants which provide a measure of relief to municipalities for loss of revenue in cases where taxable property has been acquired by federal government and thus converted into tax-free property; and grants in lieu of special assessments for local improvements.
The ordinary grants are governed by the formula which I referred to in my statement of November, 1949. Under section 125 of the British North America Act no lands or property belonging to Canada are liable to taxation. This is a sound general principle, since most federal properties exist to provide a definite service to the citizens of the communities in which they are situated. We have to realize, however, that with the expansion of functions and the growing complexity of government, concentrations of government property have developed in certain municipalities, and that in many cases these federal offices or properties serve a national or regional purpose.
It would be quite impracticable to look at every piece of federal property and decide whether or to what extent it serves primarily a local function or a regional or national function. We have therefore had to fall 80709-2682
Municipal Grants Act
back on the degree of concentration of federal property in a municipality, together with an appreciation of the burden which it imposes upon the municipality, as the test to be applied in arriving at a basis for ex gratia payments.
Our preliminary surveys indicated that, in total, federally owned properties constituted about four per cent of the value of all properties in the municipalities affected. We therefore took this four per cent as being "normal" and decided to base our grants in lieu of taxes on the amount by which the value of federal property exceeded four per cent of the value of all property in a municipality. The formula for ordinary grants set out in P.C. 741, and now incorporated in this bill, gives effect to this principle.
There are, of course, many types of federal property which confer obvious and substantial benefits on the local commqpity, such as parks, museums, irrigation works, reforestation projects, breakwaters, and aids to navigation. In respect of such properties as these the government will, of course, make no ex gratia payments to the municipalities in which they are situated.
There are also provisions for appropriate reductions in the grant in cases where the burden imposed upon the cost of municipal government by a federal property is not material, or where the government does not accept from a municipality services which the municipality customarily gives to taxable properties.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
I agree with the resolution, but I am interested in federally owned properties in the municipalities which so far at least have not been eligible to receive any of this money or these grants. I refer to a modern inland navigable canal with lands, raceways, together with buildings for weir control, bridge control, elevators, power houses, electrical buildings and so forth, which in many cases far exceed the four per cent suggested as necessary by the Minister of Finance.
Hon. members may wonder what services a municipality may have to render to a oanal. I know of some municipalities where police protection has been called so often by the canal employees and by others that the canal property has become part of the regular beat by car of the municipal police. Fire departments too are on call for fires and for drown-ings. They maintain resuscitation equipment, small boats and grappling equipment in order to recover bodies of those drowned. A dozen calls or more a year made by a fire department during a navigation season is quite a considerable service to render to a canal,
4218	HOUSE OF
Municipal Grants Act particularly when the whole fire department might be engaged in relays of four or five men each for a period of twenty-four to forty-eight hours in recovering the body of someone who has been drowned in one of the canal pondages or weirs.
In the Niagara district we have the Welland ship canal, which runs across the counties of Welland and Lincoln. It runs through the city of Welland and the towns of Port Colborne and Thorold, and several villages and townships. I admit that a fair number of people are employed in the operation of the canal, and also in the industry that has settled in the Niagara district because the canal is there. But on the other hand, many of our municipalities provide services, and they also assume much greater cost in their own operation because of the canal. I think that at least some of these costs should be assumed by the people of Canada as a whole.
With the increasing canal traffic there is much inconvenience to road and pedestrian traffic. It is acute, particularly in the city of Welland. Something better will have to be evolved to deal with this situation, which is becoming worse year by year, and it will be much aggravated when and if the St. Lawrence seaway is completed. Even now the bottleneck of traffic is very bad. I was told that in one twenty-four hour period last fall when the canal was busy the bridges were up slightly over six hours in twenty-four hours.
The city of Welland has to employ extra police to deal with this traffic. The municipalities also provide police protection to ships and to canal property generally. On frequent occasions I have seen our municipal jails and the county jails taxed to capacity by those who have violated the laws in connection with the operation of the canal. Our municipalities also provide fire-fighting services to ships and to canal property.
Our larger urban areas will require two sewage disposal plants instead of one, that is, one on each side of the canal. As hon. members know, these plants are not only expensive to build, but are costly to operate. They must also have fire-fighting equipment on each side of the canal, because of the uncertainty of being able to cross the canal on short notice. In places our townships must have two roads instead of one, a road on each side of the canal.
The present Welland canal was completed in 1931. In Port Colborne it assumed a new course. It went down through the main street. From lake Ontario to a point above Thorold it also assumed a new course in ascending the Niagara escarpment. This


means that in some places we have the present canal and the remnants of other canals. Therefore in certain areas we have much crown property held in respect of these canals.
I am not too familiar with conditions existing in other municipalities, but a year ago, when these grants were first announced, I submitted a brief to the Minister of Finance, and I am sure that this brief contained many features common to other municipalities along the Welland ship canal. For instance, in Thorold, with a total area of 1,435 acres, 500 are taken up with crown lands. About 40 acres have been turned back to the town, still leaving 450 acres of crown lands. We get no local improvement assessments in connection with streets facing the canal property, and the taxpayers maintain the roads crossing the canal property.
Around 1910 and later the government expropriated streets in the towns, in which expropriation the towns acquiesced. I cannot help but pay tribute to the business acumen of the department which has charged us for water services and power lines passing under and over some of the streets that were obtained for nothing. My mind has always been given to research, and I find that certain street allowances were afterwards sold for cash, the same streets that had been expropriated for nothing. I am not complaining about this, because I know the present Minister of Transport knew nothing about it. I could only think ill of him if this condition persists.
The Welland canal is of benefit to the people of Canada as a whole, and we feel that the people of Canada as a whole should bear some of these costs. The Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario has recognized a similar condition in the neighbouring city of Niagara Falls and the adjoining township of Stamford, because they make a payment in lieu of taxes for the power canals and the power lines running through that territory.
I appeal to the Minister of Finance to include canal property in this bill and thus give consideration to the municipalities located along the Welland ship canal.

The house resumed at three o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I was speaking of all crown agencies. I simply used those two by way of illustration.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
I quite appreciate that. I am not confining my observations to those two at all. The minister indicated that as to those two, and I take it others in a similar position, they are to be free to negotiate with the municipality to make a grant to the municipality. What will be the basis upon which the grant will be arrived at we are not told. I think it is safe to say, in the light of past experience in such matters, that they will not be paying the full taxation rate that they would be paying if they were private occupants or owners of the same property in the municipality. It seems to me that in a case of that kind, where a crown agency is directly competitive with some taxpayer, there is no reason whatever to justify this continued assumption on the part of the crown of its right to exemption from municipal taxes.


On the subject that is close to the concern and thought of many hon. members, housing, I recall the experience that many municipalities had with respect to what would have been municipal taxes on housing. Both in the case of Wartime Housing Limited and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, you will recall, Mr. Speaker, that on the properties owned by these corporations, erected by them very often on land contributed by the municipality at $1 a lot, there were no taxes payable, and all that the municipality received was a small grant in lieu of taxes. That small grant in many cases, certainly in the case of the larger urban municipalities with very heavy expenses of municipal government and the heavy cost of municipal services, had the result that they did not receive more than one-third of what they would have collected from the same properties if they had been owned by private taxpayers. There cannot be any justification for the continuation of that kind of treatment of the municipalities.
The municipalities are discharging functions that are vital. When I say that I do not mean only that many of the services they provide are essential to the conduct of civilized life, such as health, education, police and fire protection, welfare services, sewage disposal, and so on; I am thinking also of the vital contribution the municipal government makes in this country to the functioning of democracy.
For many years the costs of municipal government have been soaring, but the taxation base has remained virtually unchanged. Apart from licence fees and a few trifling incidentals, that base is confined to the taxation of real estate. With the pyramiding costs of municipal government; with more and more services demanded by the people, which services in many cases can be best and most efficiently rendered by the municipal governments, since they are closest to the people, it seems to me extremely unfair that when the federal government moves in and occupies property in the municipality, that property should be exempt from taxation. Especially is that so where it is being used for such purposes as I have mentioned, those which are competitive with the interests of private taxpayers, and those which are revenue-producing. So I say we must have regard to the fact that while the cost of municipal government has been increasing by leaps and bounds, the source of revenue has been virtually frozen. Thus when properties in these municipalities are occupied by the federal government or its agencies you have situations which are fraught with the greatest danger to the solvency of the municipalities.

I express the opinion that the formula the minister is proposing to continue does not meet the requirements of the municipalities. I do not believe it is fair or adequate, nor is it based upon a realistic appreciation of the need.
In the last analysis I suppose dollars and cents count in matters of this kind. In referring to the estimates of the department I was interested in item 127, under the heading of grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes on federal property. The minister is proposing only a slight increase this year. The estimate last year was $1,655,000 while the amount parliament is being asked to appropriate for the same purpose this year is $1,845,000, an increase of $190,000. Reference to page 173 for the details shows that of this total in 1950-51 the grants to municipalities amounted to $1,600,000. This year it is estimated that they will amount to $1,800,000, an increase of only $200,000. Measuring $1,800,000 against what the municipalities of this country lose in taxes through federal occupation of property, it seems to me that even to mention figures like that reveals at once their utter inadequacy.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, while welcoming in principle a statute to deal with this matter instead of continuing the expedient followed heretofore of passing an order in council and providing an amount in the estimates, I do urge that provision to meet the legitimate claims of the municipalities ought to be on a far more adequate scale than can possibly be the case with figures like these.

I desire to say a few words in support of the case made out this morning by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) in regard to certain lands made available to the federal government for the construction of the Welland ship canal across the Niagara peninsula. To a large extent the canals built in Canada have followed the original watercourse, but in the case of the Welland ship canal we find that the lands taken by the government cut across the face of the Niagara peninsula. These lands include many valuable fruit and farming areas, and even extend through some of the larger municipalities in that district. I refer particularly to the towns of Thorold and Port Colborne, and the city of Welland. These lands that have been taken for federal purposes are lands which otherwise would be assessable for municipal purposes. The municipalities have been deprived of their rights to levy taxes on these particular lands. The argument has been put forward that a structure such as the Welland ship canal is of great benefit to the commerce of the country, and in particular to the district in which it is located.
I believe that in addition to the great good that comes to the dominion and to the locality, the local municipalities are required to provide many services for the federal institution. One of the most costly services provided for the Welland ship canal is police protection. The northern part of the Welland ship canal passes through the township of Grantham which is in the constituency I represent. The police force maintained by the township of Grantham is, on occasion, required to spend a considerable time providing police protection for the ships, and the seamen engaged on those ships, which pass through the canal. Then, there is the matter of fire protection and life-saving services which occasion considerable expenditure. I am informed by the mayor of the city of St. Catharines that it costs the fire department $250 each time it responds to a call in the township of Grantham. It can be seen that this adds considerable expense to the municipalities concerned. In addition to that, the firemen are sometimes called to the canal for the purpose of conducting dragging operations to recover a body.
The municipalities affected are required to provide sewage disposal, and this is an additional cost. Traffic bottlenecks are created because of the canal. At Homer, on the Queen Elizabeth way, where this large traffic artery of the province of Ontario crosses the Welland canal, traffic officers are required to see that traffic moves in an orderly fashion. The same situation applies at Welland where traffic on the main street of the town is held

Municipal Grants Act
up for many hours during the day. The same condition occurs in Port Colborne. This traffic situation comes into the picture again when municipalities are required to maintain two roads, one on either side of the canal right of way.
Something has been said about the matter of income to the federal government. I believe that the federal government does derive some income from thp Welland ship canal. Within the last three or four years there has been established at Port Weller a shipbuilding plant in the drydock owned by the Department of Transport. I assume that a rental is paid. I believe it is a fine thing to have an industry of this kind, which provides employment for the people of our district, but I point this out because I believe some revenue is derived from this undertaking. Then there are canal lands which have been expropriated but which are no longer used for canal purposes. These lands have been conveyed, for a consideration, to individual owners, and I am told that in some cases the lands that were acquired at low rates have been sold at considerable profit to the department concerned. I urge the Minister of Finance, in the bill which will follow this resolution, to give consideration to providing grants for municipalities in respect of lands taken for federal purposes.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to take a rather unusual position today, inasmuch as I am not speaking for the people of Comox-Alberni but

rather as a taxpayer here in Ottawa; unfortunately I am one. I do not know who is to blame for this terrible situation we have in this city with regard to municipal taxes. If I thought it was the minister, I am afraid that I would be tempted to make a kind of rough speech; but I am not convinced that it is entirely owing to the improper basis of taxation on federal government property that is, in fact, the cause of the difficulty which we experience here.
I well appreciate the fact that the federal government provides many services to this city of Ottawa such as maintaining the parks, driveways, the museum, and all the sights we have here that cost the municipal authorities nothing. But it seems to me that the taxes here have got into the position that they are almost confiscatory. They are actually double what they are in the great city of Vancouver. I of course appreciate the fact that Vancouver does not supply the heat, the cold and the flies that we get here as part of our municipal services. But it seems to me that the federal government surely cannot be treating this town fairly when the taxes in the city of Ottawa are double what they are in the city of Vancouver.
I have a three-bedroom home out here on the federal driveway. The driveway is maintained by the federal government, but I can say that on my three-bedroom home I pay a tax of $760 a year; that is for land tax and water tax. The sum of $760 a year is a great deal of money or it used to be considered a great, deal of money. I have a colleague, also from British Columbia, who has a modest family home on a fifty-foot lot, and he pays $550 a year. I think hon. members generally do not appreciate the terrific scale of taxation that is in effect in Ottawa. Actually I am afraid that many civil servants will contemplate going up the Gatineau and putting up a wigwam, because I am almost certain that a man earning a normal salary cannot afford to pay his civic taxes.
I am not going to blame the minister for the situation. It is probably caused by a combination of circumstances. But it seems to me that the government, being the largest employers here in Ottawa, would be well advised to take an intelligent interest in this great problem that concerns every citizen of Ottawa.

As to the first question, I do not know that there is any fixed formula so far as crown corporations or agencies are concerned. They have been instructed to make with the municipalities arrangements on a fair and equitable basis. The reason for that is that the character of the operations of these crown corporations varies a good deal. For instance, the Polymer Corporation, which is in the constituency of the hon. member for Lambton West, is pretty well, one could say, an entirely commercial operation. There are, however, other crown agencies whose operations could be categorized as partly commercial and partly a general type of service. The arrangement therefore is that each crown agency negotiates its own tax arrangements with the municipality.
On the second point, as to the valuations,
I made it quite clear in my statement of November 14, 1949, that the crown must reserve to itself the right to establish the valuation. These are ex gratia payments and, for reasons which I think are fairly obvious, the crown could not put itself entirely in the hands of the local assessors. In most cases of crown property, not too much attention has been paid to the real value of the assessment because it had no practical significance in the past. But what has been done in the case of the different municipalities where grants are payable is for officials of the municipal grants division to confer with the local assessment authorities and to endeavour to arrive at an assessment which is accepted as mutually satisfactory. In one or two cases, I think here in Ottawa and in Halifax, we retained an outside real estate adviser to help in arriving at an assessment.

I should like to say a few words on this resolution. I compliment the minister and his department on the wonderful job they have done. I spent many years in municipal offices, and one of the things we had to contend with at all times was complaints based on grants in lieu of taxation, not only from the dominion government but also from the provincial government. In British Columbia we did go so far as to get grants in lieu of taxes on their property which was doing a commercial business. The only one which was placed in that particular category was the liquor stores, which are generally contained on small lots in the city or town. In my own city of New Westminster, British Columbia, I think our grant was around $27,000. That is the amount we received from the dominion government in lieu of taxes.
I do want to congratulate the minister and his department on the two civil servants who represented the department in making the final arrangements with our own city solicitor, the comptroller, mayor and council of the city. They speak of them in the highest praise. I am very sorry to hear that only a few weeks ago one of these civil servants passed away. I believe that the city's own assessor assessed the property in the neighbourhood of $30,000. The final agreement between the city assessor and the government's assessors was $27,000. The city received very favourably the amount set by the dominion government, and of those who represented the department and made the assessment they speak in the very highest praise, for the work that they have done. I think that the dominion government has taken a step in the right direction. If our provincial governments would only follow

Municipal Grants Act
they would also be taking a step in the direction that has been long needed in every municipality in the Dominion of Canada.
I am very glad to be able to rise in my place in the House of Commons and pass that praise to the department, and to those in the department who are doing that work throughout Canada. I do not think that the way it was handled in my city was any exception. All through the dominion they have done wonderful work, and I am sure they deserve all the praise that we can give them.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
There was an
amendment to this section moved by the Minister of Public Works.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure
the members of the armed forces will appreciate the concessions which have been granted in this amendment. While it was hoped that they would be granted a complete exemption from income tax, these credits will go a long way toward meeting the
Income Tax Act
situation. The only observation I desire to make is to ask assurance that the benefits granted under this bill will apply to those who receive benefits under the various pieces of legislation which have been passed in connection with members of the special force.
It will be noticed that in the amendment the zone in which these benefits will apply is described. This credit is to be given to members of the naval, army or air forces of Canada who are on duty in a zone outside Canada prescribed by regulations made on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance. I should like to direct attention to P.C. 2930 which was promulgated on Monday, June 11, and which deals with the' areas in which the benefits under such acts and regulations as the special forces veterans benefit regulations, the Veterans Rehabilitation Act, the Veterans Insurance Act and the War Service Grants Act will apply.
In those acts and regulations the area in which they are applicable is defined as being service in a theatre of operations which means such service as the governor in council may designate from time to time. P.C. 2930 goes on to define what that area is in section 1 which revokes section 3 of the special force veterans benefit regulation as follows:
For the purposes of these regulations "service in a theatre of operations" means the service of a member of the Canadian forces from the time of his departure from Canada or the continental United States of America including Alaska to participate in military operations undertaken by the United Nations to restore peace in the republic of Korea until
(a) he returns to Canada or the continental United States of America including Alaska, or
(c) the unit with which he is serving, having ceased to participate in such operations, arrives at the place to which it has been assigned,
The point I want to make is that the benefits under this amendment should apply to everybody who is taking part in these special operations. The proposed amendment will apply to everybody who is taking part in these special operations. I suggest that it might be desirable not to make it applicable to other people who are not benefiting from the veterans legislation. One does not expect these benefits to be handed out to everybody. For that reason I wanted to draw this order in council to the attention of the committee. I believe there is sufficient flexibility in the regulations so that if the 27 th brigade or other special forces go to Europe an amendment could be made to the regulations by the governor in council..

Income Tax Act
He could designate as a theatre of operations any new area overseas where Canadians were taking part.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the definition my hon. friend has indicated seems to be a pretty good one for our forces in Korea. As he has pointed out, the section in the act is drawn in such a way as to leave flexibility so that by regulation, that is to say, by order in council on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, the benefits of the section can be extended to other service personnel who may be serving outside Canada. Quite frankly I must say I have anticipated that if and when our brigade group is serving in Europe, let us say, a similar privilege would be extended to them. I agree with the hon. member that it is desirable that this benefit should at least be co-terminal with those who are eligible for veterans benefits, and it may well be that it should cover some wider ground.

As one of the first members to bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Finance earlier this session, I
want to thank him for the consideration he has given in the announcement he made not many days ago. I feel we owe this to our servicemen, and I hope it will be extended as far as reasonably possible to those men and women who may be in the fighting forces. It was a wrong that has been rectified, and I want to thank the minister for his con-* sideration.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not want to hold up my own section, but perhaps members of the committee who are interested might find it of value if I were to put on Hansard, as I do during the budget speech, tables showing the effect that this tax will have on various ranks, and with various marital statuses.
