speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
There are several points I should like to raise with respect to section 22. In the first place, it will be noted that the section applies to foreign business corporations, and the effect of subsection 1 is to require an application of the kind contemplated here to be filed within 120 days
from the end of the year. The question immediately arises: Why 120 days? The Companies Act makes a clear distinction between those companies whose business is carried on abroad and those companies whose business is domestic. I would suggest that the flat provision of 120 days from the end of the year is not entirely fair to corporations whose undertakings are largely carried on outside Canada. I should like to refer to

Income Tax Act
section 112, subsection 1, of ithe Companies Act which reads:
At each annual meeting the directors shall lay before the company
(a) a balance sheet made up to a date not more than four months before such annual meeting: Provided however that a company which carries on its undertaking out of Canada may by its bylaws extend this period to not more than six months.
I suggest in the case of such a corporation, one which carries on its undertaking outside Canada, that similar recognition should be made in this section of the difficulty cf closing its books and making its return. I would urge that in that case the time allowed should be extended to six months.
Then there is a further question. In paragraph (b) of the proposed new subsection 4 of section 64, the benefit is narrowed by these terms to companies of an industrial, mining, commercial, public utility or public service nature. I should like to ask the minister why there is any necessity for narrowing this provision to companies of these particular natures. Why should it not be made broader?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The present wording is not very narrow. This definition was put in because it was called to our attention that one or two foreign business corporations, which had their head offices in Canada and which were paying some taxes here, in fact were carrying on their operations entirely abroad, but because of a technicality they might be subject to double taxation, and under those circumstances they would be obliged to remove their offices from Canada. We could not see any particular advantage to Canada in losing the taxes which they were paying. Therefore this latter part of the amendment, subsection 4, was provided to meet these cases. As my hon. friend is aware, there are not a great many of these corporations now. They are relatively few. There are one or two very well known ones. I suppose Brazilian Traction is one of the best known.
As to the first part of my hon. friend's question concerning the 120 days or four months, that provision was in the Income War Tax Act and has not been extended. Paragraph (ii) of section 1(b) is intended to be a relieving section because under the old section as it stood after the expiry of 120 days they simply lost their right to qualify as what we used to call 4-k companies, being foreign business corporations. Now they do not lose their status as such, but if they fail to file within a certain time and in the prescribed form there is a mild penalty for failing to do so within the normal period of 120 days.
Would it not be reasonable to allow them six months?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, 120 days has always applied to these companies, and for that reason we did not think of changing it.

When you look at the
recognition given by the Companies Act to the position of such companies, would it not be reasonable to put their tax position on the same basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will have a look at it again; I confess the point had not occurred to me.
Is that the end of their calendar year or their fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The end of their fiscal year.

It seems to me the request of the hon. member for Eglinton to have the 120 days extended to six months is reasonable unless there is something against it, particularly when you consider the terms of the dominion Companies Act which seem to me sound.

Section agreed to.
Section 23 agreed to.
On section 24-Undistributed income on hand.

This relates in part to the subject matter covered by section 30, but I take it that if this section is now carried our opportunity to discuss the broad question of the distribution of these surpluses under section 30 of this bill will not be restricted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.

There is one specific point I would like to raise under subsection 5, which provides that this section shall be' deemed to have come into force on June 30,
1950.	In other words, it is made retroactive for practically twelve months, certainly ten months prior to the introduction of the budget resolutions. I am told that litigation is pending in which the definitions provided in section 24 and the new provisions there are likely to have a very direct bearing. For that reason I strongly urge that a section of this kind ought not to be made retroactive. Surely in legislation imposing taxation above all other kinds we should avoid retrospective enactment. In this case, in view of the fact that the rights of persons now engaged in litigation are likely to be affected by this enactment, I would urge that it should not be given retrospective effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am told this date was selected because it is the date on which the definition of undistributed income was brought into the act. This is a pretty technical section, as my hon. friend will appreciate, and I am told that it was discussed with the tax foundation, who felt that it was satisfactory. It is really

Income Tax Act
corrective. Some of the provisions are relieving; some might be interpreted as being more restrictive, but I think on balance it is more relieving than restrictive. I am told that the appropriate date to bring in these changes is the date on which undistributed income was defined under our act last year.
Suppose the minister were a litigant who was affected by some of the more restrictive features of this amendment and did not receive the benefit of any of the less restrictive features.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly I would not want to take away the right of anyone who is now in litigation, but the assistant deputy minister of national revenue who is sitting in front of me tells me he does not know of any such case and certainly I had none under consideration when this section was being prepared. It was not intended to legislate anybody out of their rights. Of course it only affects undistributed income.

Someone spoke to me the
other day, indicating that the rights of his clients were going to be affected by the retrospective operation of this amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would be surprised if that were the case. If my hon. friend wants it to stand I have no objection, but I would hope that we might pass it.

I do not wish to hold anything up at this stage of the session, but after all what purpose can there be in enacting retroactive legislation now simply because of the definitions introduced last year? It does not seem to me we should go back and change the definition as of that date.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Sections such as these are introduced as a rule because of representations made to us that this should be done. This section in fact reflects the departmental practice since this question of undistributed income was first defined in last year's act, and I really would be very much surprised if any matter now in litigation would be prejudicially affected by the provisions of this section.

Section agreed to.
On section 25-Mining companies.

I would like to urge the
minister, in preparing his budget next year, to make some similar provision for those who are practising forest conservation and silviculture, because these are the people who will be providing wealth for future generations, from which they themselves will receive no direct benefit at the present time. I know the government is conscious of the need for forest conservation. So are many
people across Canada, and I do believe something should be done to assist those individuals who are doing something to benefit future generations. They are expending money which will bring them no direct benefit, and I feel that those people undertaking forest conservation are doing something very worth while. We know we have to protect our forests if we are to have a consistent yield of forest products. We have to protect them if we are to protect our water resources; and we have to protect our forests if we are to prevent land erosion through floods. Some exemption from taxation for those willing to do this sort of work on behalf of future generations would be a good investment because it would bring the country wealth in later years. It would also be a good investment because large sums of money would be saved which otherwise would have to be expended to repair water damage and soil erosion as the result of overcutting. I would like the minister to give his opinion on this suggestion, but before he does so I believe another hon. member would like to say a few words on the matter.

I know the minister has had this question and the lack of a forest policy for Canada brought to his attention already, and certainly I do not want to take the time of the house unnecessarily in presenting a point I believe his experts are studying now. I only want to point out that British Columbia is recognizing the fact that we must encourage people to plant timber for future generations. The provincial minister of mines and forests introduced a resolution at this session of the British Columbia legislature which provided for a two-thirds reduction in taxation on land which the owners would undertake to use as forest farms, and I should think the government here would be well advised to go along with that policy and cooperate in every possible way in this worthwhile project.
It is generally assumed down here, of course, that anyone taking up a forest management licence in British Columbia is getting something of great value and that as a result their capital interest in timber must be increased. Actually that is hardly the case. At the present time if the owners of standing timber in British Columbia enter into one of these forest management licences they must expect to have their present cutting rights abridged to a very great extent. It is only their realization that in the public interest they have a responsibility that could possibly justify their entering one of these contracts, because certainly the present generation will get no personal benefit. I was rather shocked to learn, as a

Income Tax Act
matter of fact, that the Department of National Revenue was imposing taxation on funds expended by timber companies in British Columbia on the mapping and planning of these forest management licences. It seems to me that is entirely inconsistent with the policy announced in this house by the Minister of Resources and Development, who said we were going to set aside $2 million for the purpose of assisting the provinces to take a forest inventory. I think we should co-operate with the provincial governments in every possible way, and with regard to timber we should take the same attitude that we take to oil and minerals. I would ask that the minister give this matter his usual able consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I did mention at the resolution state-and if I did not I do so now-that this very important question is now being considered by my colleague the Minister of Resources and Development, and I believe he has been having some discussions with the provinces about it.
I am very pleased to hear that.

Section agreed to.
On section 26-Right to file consolidated return.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have a small amendment which I would ask one of my colleagues to move. It is to substitute in subsection 4 the following: "This section is applicable to the year 1952 and subsequent taxation years."

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I move accordingly.
Amendment agreed to.

I am glad the minister has amended this section in one respect, and I very much hope he may amend it in another. I am troubled indeed that the right to file a consolidated return is to be done away with. We have had no explanation as to why this is being done. I am going to ask the minister to give an explanation, and then I wish to say something more. First I want to draw attention to two or three vital points in that connection. This is a right which has existed since 1932. I imagine we will all agree that if it is withdrawn now it will be extremely difficult to ever reinstate it. This practice has been followed by a considerable number of corporations, and they have actually paid an additional rate of two per cent for the privilege. Before I go any farther I wish the minister would give us the reasons for making this important change.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The principal reason of course is that, now we have introduced into the act the principle of carrying losses forward and backward, this has ceased to have the practical significance it used to have. Only in the case of a consistent loser would it be of any benefit. In the case of companies jointly controlled, having one company that never made anything and another one that nearly always did, there would be some advantage in consolidating and paying the extra two per cent in respect thereto. It was thought desirable to eliminate this provision from the act. There is no desire to penalize the comparatively few companies that are still availing themselves of this privilege. It is for that reason I am proposing that it shall not be applicable except to the 1952 and subsequent periods. This will provide ample time for such companies as are still using this privilege to make proper arrangements so that they will not be unduly penalized.
I may say thait the amendment to become effective in 1952 was introduced as a result of representations made to me that it might be difficult for one or two companies to so re-arrange their affairs that they would not be penalized.

I am still bothered by this, because as I gathered from the minister he does not regard it as a very important matter. He has not give any overwhelming reason for the change, and I should like to answer the reason he has given, because I have representations on that point to the following effect.
The general assumption that the introduction of loss carry-over provisions has eliminated the advantage of consolidated returns is no doubt substantially correct so far as a comparison of aggregate revenue yields is concerned. But it does not apply to certain advantages of a more technical character, as in cases where consolidation permits separate incorporation of a certain part of a business for reasons of provincial law, or meets the case of a chronic loser. In such cases the use of consolidated returns allows flexibility of corporate organization which may be advisable for reasons of business where tax considerations are secondary. Again I want to put this point to the minister.
I am doing it because it does seem to me a case where the point is substantial, and unless there is a great balance of convenience I hope the minister will listen.
The next point I wish to make is connected with the proposed repeal of section 75. As I understand it, that is not dictated by calculation of alternative revenue yields, and it is therefore primarily a matter of administrative convenience. If that is the

correct inference, I would strongly urge that the convenience and established practice of the taxpayers concerned, whoever they may be, should receive at least equal consideration before this amendment proceeds further. May I earnestly say to the minister that it seems to me the reasons that have been given are not at all conclusive. Unless some real disadvantage is suffered by the public service, surely the convenience of the long-suffering taxpayer could receive some consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I considered these questions because of similar representations made to me by the tax foundation. I felt that, on balance, this was a case where we should do away with this provision.

I must express regret at the decision made by the minister. However, if he is not prepared to change his mind I shall pass to another point on this section. Has the minister noted the form of the draftsmanship of this section? Where is this section going to go in the act? It does not purport to be amending any section in the act at the present time. All it does is repeal section 75, and then it goes on to enact a new provision without indicating where it is to go in the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Section 75, of course, of the act which is repealed is the section giving the right to file consolidated returns. This section 26, subsection 2, will not go into the Income Tax Act at all. It is purely a transitional provision. It will provide for the clearing up of matters by the companies who have been filing under this right. During 1952 and subsequent periods, section 75 will cease to be in the act.

Section agreed to.
Sections 27 to 29 inclusive agreed to.
On section 30-Corporation election.

Section 30 is a very
important section. I believe there is a number of points that are likely to arise under this section. This is the section by which the government proposes to extend in one case, and narrow in another, the right given to corporations last year to distribute surpluses on the payment of a 15 per cent tax thereon. On the one hand I believe the committee will agree with the minister in his budget statement that the amendment made last year in the enactment of section 95A fully justified itself in the use made of it. Undoubtedly more use was made of it than the minister contemplated at that time, because the device of incorporating stockholding companies for the purpose of qualifying as private corporations
Income Tax Act
with no more than 75 shareholders was hardly foreseen last year by the minister, and certainly the wide use that has been made of it. In proposing now to extend this right more widely, I believe the minister is only recognizing what has largely become an established fact.
At the same time, one wonders why the minister selects a broad class of corporations as an exception to what has now become the general rule that any corporation may distribute its accumulated surplus. This exception is found in subsection 2, lines 36 and 37 of the bill, and instead of being a private corporation as defined by the act, namely one having not more than 75 shareholders, these narrowing words are used:
A corporation other than a subsidiary controlled corporation.
So that there are no benefits to be extended to a corporation where the dominant shareholder is a corporation. But I think that this exception, made to what has now become the general rule, does not adequately take into account the position of minority shareholders. These minority shareholders may be large in number. It may be that the control held by one dominant corporation is a very tenuous measure of control indeed, yet in such a case the position of the minority shareholders receives no consideration whatever under this legislation. As a matter of fact, I think one could go further and say that corporations which derived benefit under this section will now lose it under the narrowing provisions of this amendment. I can think of a number of corporations which acquired the right to pay the 15 per cent tax on distributed surpluses last year which will lose that right under this amendment.
For that reason, Mr. Chairman, I would urge that if the provision has justified itself, as the minister indicated in his budget speech, and as I think most people recognize, then there is no reason for introducing this qualification. Why not make it general, and in that way avoid doing injustice to the minority shareholders? There are other aspects of this matter which I should like to discuss, but perhaps it would be more orderly if we took them one at a time.

May I add
a word before the minister answers the member for Eglinton. I should like to endorse as strongly as I can what the member for Eglinton has said. It seems to me that this section is discriminatory to a high degree against minority shareholders; in other words, against people who are apt to be the small holders. Unless there is some overwhelming reason for it, I do not think there is

Income Tax Act
any justification, as you are leaving the minority shareholders, perhaps 49 per cent of the corporation, with what was a valuable right, conveyed so short a time ago, now entirely destroyed. I earnestly hope that the minister will see his way clear to deal with the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As my hon. friend appreciates, it is a loophole provision. There is a wide-open street there which we were afraid, without too great difficulty, could be made the subject of great abuse. This was a new provision introduced last year. As members of the committee have said, it introduced a special privilege to enable the distribution of surpluses on payment of a 15 per cent tax. I think it was a desirable piece of legislation. It has now been extended to public companies. It may be, to use the language of the tax foundation report, that the weight of the plug may be out of proportion to the size of the loophole, and we are prepared to explore alternative measures that can be entertained at this stage.
I will be prepared to pursue alternative measures. I have not been able to find anything yet; so that at this time I think that this is a provision which must be inserted in the act.

I wish the minister would
be more explicit. I do not think he has covered the whole ground by any means.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have done the best I can.

On this point I have more confidence in the minister than he apparently has in himself. I think he can do better.
Speaking of loopholes, obviously the 1950 legislation left a great big loophole. I doubt greatly if the department foresaw the loophole there was in the 1950 legislation. The fact of the matter is that the minister derived a great deal of revenue from the fact that there was a great big loophole. If I am not mistaken, his revenue from this source, this new section 95A, was about $95 million in the last fiscal year. It contributed greatly to the surplus which the minister was able to report to the house in his budget speech. Much of the surplus is attributable to the fact that a loophole was left in last year's legislation.
I am sure that every lawyer in the house is aware of the loophole, Mr. Chairman, because the right was confined to private corporations, and they were defined as corporations having no more than 75 shareholders. A great many incorporations resulted for the purpose of consolidating stock

ownership, in order to bring the stock ownership within the definition of a private corporation. So let us not be too seriously talking now about a loophole. It was last year's loophole that was the big one, and the minister's budget was the beneficiary of that loophole.
The minister accepts the principle of last year's legislation. He says he approves it to the point where he is prepared to extend it more widely. He therefore proposes to eliminate altogether the requirement of last year's legislation that it be confined to corporations having no more than 75 shareholders. But then he comes along and proposes to take away the right from some corporations that already have it, having qualified last year as private corporations. He proposes to take that right away from them this year. Surely if the principle were sound last year, it is sound this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is for the future, not for the past.
Oh, yes. I appreciate the fact that this provision is not retroactive. It does not have to answer for that additional vice. We will acquit it of that charge.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The matching provision does not apply to this type of corporation in the future.

All right. There is the point. I say that if the principle of last year's legislation was sound, and if it is so sound that it deserves quite wide extension as is proposed in this amendment, then I cannot for the life of me see that the minister has made out any case for carrying that extension to the point where he not only withdraws it from some corporations which would acquire it this year but also withdraws it from some that acquired it under last year's legislation. It seems to me that he has not taken account at all, in his explanation, of the position of the minority shareholders in those cases. It may be that the minister has some legitimate concern which he has not yet expressed to the committee as to the position of the majority or dominant shareholders in a case of that kind where one corporation holds the control of the other. But he has not dealt with the question of the position of the minority shareholders, and it may be an important one in that particular company. It seems to me that they are the people who are deserving of the utmost consideration in a case of this kind.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to be persistent enough also to have another go at this matter. It seems

to me that what is happening is that by reason of the chance of abuse the minister is -ready to accept the certainty of doing a grave injustice to a considerable number of people of the kind that most deserve the protection of this committee, namely the smaller people in the main. I am not suggesting for a moment that the minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is almost certainly abuse.

I have considerable confidence in the minister's staff. The minister says there is almost certainly abuse. I will not quibble about words. I will say to him that there is an absolute certainty-no doubt whatever-that as it is now an injustice is being done to the minority shareholders. Will the minister say there is a hardship where I called it an injustice? Is the minister agreed that there is a hardship?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. I do not think there is a hardship. Minority shareholders are always subject to certain disabilities and this may happen to be one of them.

Oh, I do not
think that that answers the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows just as well as I do what is going to happen; or if he does not, he is the only man in Canada who does not. This matching legislation was designed with the idea in mind that half of the profits of the corporation would be distributed and be subject to tax and the other half could be created as a tax-free surplus by paying 15 per cent. If the situation of a parent and subsidiary is involved what happens is this. Half is distributed in accordance with the provision of the act as it now stands. It goes to the parent but it does not pay any tax unless the parent should see fit to distribute that. It is only the remaining half of which some may happen to go to the minority shareholders

if there are minority shareholders. The remaining half pays tax at the rate of 15 per cent. So you could have a situation where the only tax that would be paid would be 15 per cent and the parent could accumulate and accumulate on that basis. That never was intended; and unless I can find some other way of making sure that it cannot be done, that provision cannot stay in this section. If, incidentally, some minority shareholders are inconvenienced, that is unfortunate. But certainly they are no worse off than they were before this section was put into this act.

I do not think the minister has answered my point at all. I accept his rebuke if he wishes to give it. But
Income Tax Act
it does not affect the point at all. It simply means that-I will not say because no effort has been made, for of course some effort has been made-because they have not yet finally found a satisfactory way of doing it, these people have to suffer.

If the minister's heart is not to be warmed on that point, I will try him on another one. This is a point that I think must be within the minister's knowledge as having arisen under last year's legislation. It is a point of some difficulty. When the minister brought in his legislation a year ago he intimated-in fact I think he said this on several occasions-that the way in which the corporation, having paid this 15 per cent tax on that undistributed surplus, could then effect distribution among the shareholders, was through such forms as stock bonus, issuance of preferred stock and so on. I do not think that due account could have been taken at the time of the effect of one provision of the Companies Act on this matter. I believe this problem has arisen in the experience of a number of companies. As I understand it, the idea back of section 95A was to eliminate a surplus as a surplus and to effect distribution. Of course there are many corporations which did not have preferred stock or did not have the right to issue preferred stock, which in the meantime have *acquired that right, have issued preferred stock, have made their election, paid their 15 per cent and wish to distribute by way of redemption, in whole or in part, of preferred stock where the preferred stock was issued in amounts equal to the amount of the surplus heretofore undistributed, now distributable by paying 15 per -cent tax. They run up against the provisions of section 61 of the Companies Act, in the case of dominion corporations. I am sorry to bring in a long section -in a technical discussion, Mr. Chairman, but I think I have to quote most of this rather long -section to the minister to illustrate the point, which is this: While the purpose of the legislation was to eliminate what had been undistributed surplus from the company's balance sheet as a surplus, as I understood it, nevertheless it seems to me that the effect of section 61 of the Companies Act, as applied to companies incorporated under that act or subject to it, is to prevent that surplus from being removed from the balance sheet of the company-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I interrupt my hon.
friend to make a brief comment? The purpose of the section was to facilitate capitalization of an earned surplus. It was not necessarily or primarily intended to facilitate

Income Tax Act
the distribution of the capitalized surplus if it had been capitalized. I know that in fact in law it has not been too difficult to effect that distribution, but the primary purpose was not to facilitate an easy distribution; it was to facilitate an easy capitalization without attracting too high a tax.

I think that some of us
formed a quite different impression from the statements that were made last year, and certainly when wide publicity was given to the new section 95A it was done on the basis of this provision now making it possible to effect distribution tax-free of-

speechtext:
I did not make the publicity

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Well, it is some little time
since I have been able to earn a modest living by giving advice on these matters, but I did assume when we introduced this legislation last year that the capitalized surplus could only be withdrawn by way of a reduction of capital under sections 49 and following of the Companies Act. It was not then intended that it should be automatically paid out as dividends. The main underlying purpose of the legislation was to enable earnings which in fact had been reinvested in the business and were shown on the company's balance sheet as an unearned surplus of capital, and under the proper circumstances, to be withdrawn from the company.
From what I have seen and heard, while we may have given a little extra work to the members of parliament in the accounting and legal profession, I must say that it has not proved an insuperable difficulty to get out this capital surplus if it is desired to do so. Mind you, I think that in most cases where this surplus has been capitalized there has been no intention of withdrawing it from the company. I think that in a good many cases it has been necessary to leave it in there as working capital, or as a reinvestment in the business, but it was desirable, in order to eliminate the double punitive taxation features of succession duties and income taxes, to provide this way of dealing with that capitalized undistributed surplus.

It may be that what the minister has had to say today does clarify the situation, although it is not the interpretation that was widely put on the remarks the minister made last year in indicating the purpose of the section, because under what has become the common practice now, where preferred stock was issued following the election under 95A, and the companies now are proceeding to redeem that preferred stock in whole or in part, they cannot even by the fact of that redemption effect the reduction in surplus that I think it was generally felt they could.

I should like to go back to the discussion we were having last Wednesday when this came up and when the minister explained to us what had happened since the making of the budget speech. I want to read to the minister what he said in his budget speech which to me appeared to be departed from in the budget resolutions. 1 am doing this because I think if the matter is left as it is now it will create a serious situation indeed and one which I hope we can persuade the minister to consider seriously. The minister is reported on page 1810 of Hansard as saying:
I am conscious of the fact, however, that this 20 per cent surcharge will weigh very heavily on those kinds of companies which for a variety of reasons, public control of rates or otherwise, are never able to earn more than a very modest rate on their capital. To such companies the next few years can offer little expectation of increased profits, yet many of them are engaged in activities which will require them to raise very large sums of additional capital for essential expansion.
I draw the minister's attention to that because my belief is that as matters stand that will be almost impossible of accomplishment. The minister continued:
If we are not to cripple their borrowing capacity we must not cripple their capacity to earn their normal profits after tax. For these reasons I propose that the 20 per cent defence surcharge shall not operate so as to reduce the net income after federal tax, but before any provincial income taxes, of any company to a point below a five per cent return on capital employed.
Then I should like to refer to last Wednesday when the minister said:
I found I simply could not evolve a definition which would be fair to all taxpayers. Therefore I am reluctantly forced to drop what I hoped might be a relieving provision.
I want to emphasize at the outset that what I am concentrating on is the minister's statement of April 10 when he spoke about utility corporations, particularly when he pointed out first of all the narrowness of their earnings which in a great many cases are fixed by regulating boards so that there is just, enough to carry on with, and second, when he pointed out that they were going to need great expansion and would have to be in a position where their borrowing power was not crippled. I might add here that I think the Minister of Defence Production has been at great pains to indicate the importance of public utilities and the necessity of their expansion.
It is with that in mind that I wish to make certain representations to the minister. I

want to emphasize again the position of utility companies if the matter stands as it is now. In most cases they are just getting enough earnings. They will have to apply for increased rates if the matter stands as it is. The increased rates which they will have to charge will just be added on to the cost of living and will be another addition to the inflationary pressure. First of all I want to ask the minister if he agrees so that we shall see whether we have a common basis. I want to ask the minister whether he agrees that if the matter stands as it is now there will of necessity be applications for increased rates. I also want to ask him if he agrees that corporations will be in the ironical position where they will really have to ask for $2 for every $1 that the minister is going to get because of the fact that they only get half of their earnings anyway. The tax is now up to 50 per cent. In other words, if a company has to raise money to pay the surcharge, if it has to apply for additional rates, it will have to get $2 for every $1. I should like to know whether the minister accepts that view because what I want to go on to say is to some extent based on that proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course public utility companies are no different from any other company in theory so far as the imposition of corporation taxes is concerned. Those taxes must be passed on to the purchaser of the service or the goods of the corporation which pays the tax. In the case of public utility corporations they have to go to a board, some public body, to get an authorized rate increase. In the case of commercial corporations they have to add it on to the price, or squeeze their profits and dividends a bit, or both. However, in essence what people should always realize is that the corporation tax has to be paid by the people who buy the service of the corporation or who buy the products that it manufactures. That is the only way it can be paid. The corporation has not any money except what it obtains from the people to whom it sells its goods. If it does not at least sell for its costs and a reasonable return on its capital, then over a period of time I suppose the inevitable happens as it has in other places and it goes bankrupt. There is nothing new about that. Of course I agree with my hon. friend.
I am grateful that the minister agrees with me although he took quite a long while to say yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I am conscious of the fact, however, that this 20 per cent surcharge will weigh very heavily on those kinds of companies which for a variety of reasons, public control of rates or otherwise, are never able to earn more than a very modest rate . . .
That is the great and very important difference, just as he has pointed out, between those companies and companies which are not restricted in that way. As we all know, those companies which come before boards are usually allowed just enough to get by, and just as soon as they have extra charges then they are in trouble. Then I want to come to the point which the minister makes that it is not possible to find a definition to deal with the situation. That is the thing that I do not like to accept, and which I do not think we should accept, because I think it is far too serious for the whole economy of the country.
The minister says he has been unable to work out a definition of capital employed which would be satisfactory from the point of view of its general application to all companies. I am talking particularly, as I said, about utility companies, and that is what I want to emphasize. I do not believe it would be difficult to devise a definition to apply to public utilities which is the field most pressingly involved, and which by the nature of the budget address it was chiefly intended to cover. We have a very useful precedent in the United States because earlier this year the United States congress had to meet the same-problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is under the excess profits tax act of the United States?

Yes, I will come to that. I will make that clear. Congress stipulated that electrical, gas, telephone, transit and water utilities were exempt from the provisions of the excess profits -tax act, which the 20 per cent surcharge takes the place of in Canada, up to 6 per cent return on capital employed in the case of all but telephone and gas utilities where the allowed return was 7 per cent. I come to what I think.

Income Tax Act
is the most important point of all. The definition of return on capital employed covered dividend requirements of common and preferred shares, interest on bonded indebtedness and surplus. The same sort of treatment would meet the requirements of the public utilities in Canada that the minister has been talking about, and it is no less essential for the war preparedness effort here than it is in the United States.
When this matter came up last Wednesday the minister spoke as if it might work into possibly a major reconstruction of our tax system next year, but what I want to represent to the minister is that the present situation is going to create a difficult if not impossible situation this year. I hope the minister will agree, and if he does not I think it is desirable that he should say so, that the utilities will have to raise millions of dollars of new capital this year as well as next, and anyone who has any knowledge of the capital markets appreciates that the monetary policy against inflation that the country has been following since April makes it more difficult than previously to raise new capital through bonds and preferred stocks. To apply a 20 per cent surcharge to utilities would so depress their earnings as to make it impossible for them to raise capital through the sale of common stock this year.
When I say "impossible" that is perhaps a strong word. I am speaking of the difficulties which it is reasonable to take into account, and I come back again and again to emphasize the minister's own words. I submit again that if the minister had confined himself to the objective which he laid down in April with regard to utilities the problem would have been a very different one, and that we might not have had the minister coming to us last Wednesday and confessing failure.
There is another point that I should make. Inevitably we are going to have a demand for increased rates which will bear hard on everybody, and even then the situation will not be wholly cured because the increased rates probably will not become effective in the immediate future. Therefore I put it to the minister that the present situation is one that he cannot possibly tolerate with equanimity, and that to merely say it cannot be done and leave it at that is to fail to deal with a problem which I think cries out for a solution. I suggest to the minister that our problem is the same as the problem they had in the United States, and that mutatis mutandis the solution which has worked there might very well work here.

I thought when the minister brought down his budget that this abatement of the 20 per cent surcharge was a wise

provision, and I still think so. It is particularly wise, I think, when we begin to apply it to the group of corporations in the country known as utilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought my hon. friend wias asking me to increase the corporation tax.

Not at all; not on this part. I have always had in mind this abatement provision and the 5 per cent. I think the minister knows that quite well. Certainly I agreed with him and with all those who took the position that in no case should we tax corporations to a point where they would net less than a fair percentage on the capital employed. I realize all too well how difficult it is to determine in formal language and for all corporations the meaning of capital employed, but a suggestion was just made by the hon. member for Greenwood which I think is wise and quite possible of application here. That is the definition as laid down in the United States under the excess profits tax, which provides that in the case of utilities there are three component parts to the capital employed, the share capital, the bonded indebtedness and the surplus. Certainly it should be possible to spell out in any amendment a specification of that kind applying particularly to utilities, so I would ask the minister to give very careful consideration to including for this year at least the provision of the abatement principle for utilities, if not for all corporations.
I should like to emphasize a little more one point made by the hon. member for Greenwood. If the abatement provision is withdrawn, as the minister suggests he is going to withdraw it, not only will it be necessary for many of the utilities to apply to the public service commissions for increases in rates. It will also be necessary for many of those corporations to wait for months before they can apply any such increase. As everyone knows it takes all the the way from three to six, seven or eight months to get permission from a provincial commission to apply a new rate, and in the meantime these utilities are going to suffer. They will be put in a very embarrassing position, and this at a time when the Minister of Defence Production is asking them to go all out to aid defence production. It does not seem to me that the two ministers are quite in accord. Certainly I would suggest that the Minister of Finance give careful consideration to the case that has been presented by the hon. member for Greenwood, and I support his request that for this year at any rate the abatement principle be applied to the utilities and that capital employed be defined as has been suggested, to include bonded indebtedness, surplus, and share capital.

respect of income earned after the commencement of the 1951 calendar year a corporation shall pay a defence surtax equal to 20 per cent, subject to the provision that the tax should not reduce the corporation's taxable Income after payment of ordinary income tax to an amount less than 5 per cent of the capital employed. by regulation, it ought to be possible to do it with equal facility by statute. But the minister invites the committee to accept his conclusion that it is not possible to prepare a definition of the expression "capital employed."

All right, to define it satisfactorily. There is no quarrel on that; it is a matter of terms. I would be the first one to recognize the difficulty facing the minister in working out a satisfactory general definition to apply to all cases. But I do not think we can accept that as sufficient ground for repudiating a decision taken by the house, a decision that was an essential feature of the budget proposals of the minister. In justifying this second increase in the corporation tax within about nine months, the minister laid great stress on the fact that it was not going to prevent any corporation from earning a rate of five per cent on its employed capital. Unquestionably, there are difficulties. Anyone who had any experience with our Excess Profits Tax Act will not be unaware of the difficulties of defining capital employed.
But I submit we must go on with this problem, and find a satisfactory definition of capital employed. For the sake of bringing that about, I am prepared to curb my own objections in order to provide the minister and his advisers with sufficient time. I do urge that the problem should not be treated in the way the minister invites us in his amendment to do, simply admit defeat and cast out a saving provision which was an integral part of the general proposal for an increase in corporation taxes. The member for Greenwood and the member for Peace River have quite rightly stated that if you do not add such a saving provision as this in the case of public utilities, then inevitably those public utilities are going to have to go to the boards that set their rates and make applications for increases. One of the things that will happen will be another application by the railways of this country to the board of transport commissioners for another increase in freight rates. The same will be true of the Bell Telephone Company, and other public utilities that are subject to the jurisdiction of provincial boards in practically every province in this country. The public is going to be called upon to pay.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, we are not going to accept defeat in a matter so important. Surely, we are not going to perpetuate a situation now by means of which we are going to embark on a program of repudiating decisions of this house. We must now tell the public

utilities up and down this country that if they are going to maintain the rate of return on their employed capital-it is not a very large return at best-then they shall have to launch their applications now for an increase in rates. It is just as inflationary as it can be, and it is going to defeat many of the pleas that the Minister of Defence Production is making to these corporations to expand their output.
Let us recall what the Minister of Finance said in his budget speech, that the next few years could offer little expectation for increased profits, yet many of the companies are engaged in activities which require them to raise very large sums of additional capital for essential expansion. With the curbs there are on credit now, that additional capital for essential expansion is not going to be available to those companies. I urge the minister not to be content to accept defeat in his efforts to bring about a satisfactory definition of employed capital. The committee recognizes the difficulties. No one who knows anything about this problem will underestimate the difficulties with which we are faced, but surely we are not going to admit we cannot work out a definition, given the time and the opportunity of consultation with the advisers of the government and others. I would urge that in something so important, so integral a feature of the budget proposals of the minister, this committee should insist that the scheme of those proposals be proceeded with, and that a definition be worked out. This would enable the decision of the house to be implemented.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is really nothing I can add to what I said the other night on the technical point raised by the hon. member. The government's budgetary proposals are always subject to revision until the acts implementing them are finally passed by the house. It is true that it is fairly rare for a minister of finance to suggest taking away something he hoped to be able to give to some taxpayers; that happens to be the case here. More often some additional concession is given, as is the case in the special tax exemption for the armed forces. No one regrets more than I do that it has not been possible to evolve' a satisfactory definition which would be fair to all taxpayers. As I said the other day, we have made extended efforts to do so and we have failed. So far as I am concerned I can only say to the house that for this coming year, for the reasons I have given, the twenty per cent surcharge will apply to all corporations who have profits during the year.

I would be interested in hearing the minister's reply to the suggestion

made by the hon. member for Greenwood concerning the taxation of public utilities. Would it not be generally better to put public utilities in a different taxation set-up from the ordinary company? Probably the minister will confirm this, but I have always felt that British Columbia suffered a greater disability, since most of the public utilities are privately owned, than the people of Ontario where they have the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That, of course, is a situation which has existed for some time. It is true not only of the province of British Columbia but also of the province of Quebec, where we have large privately owned utilities. We now have some that are publicly owned. In the province of Ontario power interests are principally publicly owned, but that is not true of telephone companies. Power companies are perhaps entirely publicly owned, with the exception of some in northern Ontario. There is no doubt it would be desirable to try to evolve some tax plan which might be more equitable. As my hon. friend appreciates, there are considerable difficulties. Perhaps a fairer way might be to put the load directly on the consumers instead of collecting it through the corporation tax. Some hon. members have expressed concern that the new tax deduction tables, which are to become effective as from July 1, 1951, provide for greater deductions than the 20 per cent defence surtax. Similar complaints have been received from outside quarters. First of all, let me state definitely that the tax itself is not increased by one cent more than my colleague the Minister of Finance announced in his budget address. However, the proportion of the tax that is collected in the least painful way, that is, at the source, from wages and salaries, has been increased.
Barely two months ago, many editorials and news stories called attention to and criticized the department because large balances of taxes were payable by wage earners last April. Generally speaking, these payments ranged from $15 to $25 per person, and in the aggregate they totalled about $40 million, to be paid largely out of the pockets of the working people at that time.
The feeling may have developed during the years after the war, when taxes were declining, that there was a strong tendency towards the creation of overpayments, although this tendency was not fostered by the basis of tax deduction. There seems to be little doubt that the wage earner prefers that his tax be paid as fully as possible by deductions at the source. The department subscribes to this view, but it was not deemed practicable to issue a new and slightly higher table of deductions until such time as a
Income Tax Act
general adjustment of taxes was before parliament. There were two sound reasons for this. First, a change of this nature places a severe strain on the payroll operation of all employers-large or small-and it is desirable that the number of such changes should be kept to an absolute minimum. Secondly, the employee would in many cases interpret the change to be an increase in tax imposed by my department without sanction of parliament.
When the budget was brought down this year, necessitating the issuance of a new set of tables, the opportunity for revising the basis presented itself. It was realized, however, that circumstances were not wholly favourable because, for a majority of persons, the deduction per pay period would increase by more than 20 per cent. On the other hand, we were confronted with the fact that the year-end balances would automatically be 20 per cent higher in the future if we did not do something about it immediately.
A careful study was made of all the factors bearing on the problem and it was decided to recast the tax deduction tables in such a way that the least possible amount should be left to be paid at the end of the year, but that in the process no person should deliberately have an over-deduction made at the source. The steps taken to accomplish this were, first of all, to narrow the range of the income brackets within which a specified amount of tax deduction was to apply. When the income bracket is narrowed, the tax deduction becomes more precise. Secondly, the amount of tax specified for a given bracket was the full amount payable for the income which constituted the bottom of the bracket-that is the highest level. For an income which is in the middle of the bracket, the rate of deduction falls slightly short of 100 per cent of the tax payable; while at the top of the bracket, the deduction is still further short of the full tax. That is, we range it for an income that runs from $40 to $50 a week.
The average weekly wage across Canada in February, 1951, was $47.76, according to the dominion bureau of statistics. In the new tax deduction table, this wage falls within the weekly bracket $47.50 to $48.49. That is the dollar range. There will be shown the percentage deduction, the balance payable at the end of the year and the amount of charitable donations, over and above any investment income that might be earned, that would be required to convert the balance payable into a refund.

The money is in the hands of the government and it is the old story that when the government owes you money, you do not get interest, but when you owe the government money, you pay interest. I think this objectionable position could be corrected, by making alterations on this form.

We will look into the matter raised by the hon. member for Hamilton West. It is just as hard for the taxpayer to anticipate what his medical expenses will be as it is to anticipate what his increased income may be.

That may be, provided
you do not have a specific instance. If you know that someone in your family has gone to hospital, if you know how long he may be there and how much you must pay per week, plus the surgery bills, you can make an estimate of the money you will have to spend before the end of the year.

I think the statement made
by the Minister of National Revenue has
Income Tax Act
been useful and I am glad he has given us such an extended statement. However, I think he has revealed a more stringent approach to the problem than some of us had supposed would be made. I am not going to criticize the department for breaking down the present categories with a view to narrowing them. That is a perfectly reasonable approach. But when we find deductions scheduled to take 99-9 per cent of the income tax in certain categories, it seems to me that that is going too far. That is the whole basis of my reaction to the statement.
The fact is that you are going to create a great deal more work in the department and add to the administrative tasks of those who review the applications for refunds. It is going to mean that far more people are going to be overpaid than has hitherto been the case. In the meantime they will have to forgo interest, and wait until the department makes a refund. I agree that the department is showing better results in connection with refunds, but there is no sense in trying to extend these deductions to the point where inevitably you are going to increase the number of overpayments and the consequent applications for refund.

Instead they have provided for its being pushed up by 73 per cent. It seems to me quite obvious that the department is going too far in this matter. speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: MODIFICATION OF APPLICATION AS TO LAST QUARTER OF 1950 AND EXTENSION IN MODIFIED FORM TO 1951
speechtext:
Yes. At the resolution stage we had a very comprehensive and constructive debate. The speeches were on a high level, and many helpful suggestions were made. I had prepared a rather full statement for delivery at this second reading stage, but at the insistence of the opposition I was persuaded to put it on the record at that time. My colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will make a statement covering the international monetary fund and free market aspects of the problem. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, and with the consent of hon. members I would ask that his statement follow immediately upon the conclusion of my remarks.
During the time that has elapsed since the first reading of this bill we have undertaken a very careful review of the whole situation, and as a result of our study the government is now prepared to propose in the committee stage an amendment that will broaden the application of cost aid and give further assistance to the gold mines. Hon. members will recall that on the introduction of Bill No. 194 to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, certain questions were raised in respect to possible decreased payments to British Columbia lode gold mines as a result of the revision of the formula to be applied this year, 1951. The recent change in the formula for 1951, as in the bill now before the house, allows for payments on more assistance ounces than the original formula; and, assuming a similar production in 1951 as in 1950, it is estimated that five mines in British Columbia namely Bralorne, Cariboo Gold Quartz, Island Mountain, Kelowna Exploration and Pioneer, will be paid in 1951 on 103,250 assistance ounces in comparison with 98,086 assistance ounces in 1950, an estimated increase of 4-2 per cent in the number of ounces. In the British Columbia submission received by a number of hon. members, Polaris Taku was included. It is

understood that this mine is being closed and the mill being taken over by other operators. It will thus receive payments for only a small production of 1951 previous to the cessation of operations. For this reason it is here omitted for comparative purposes of payments in 1950 and 1951.
Assuming that the production of the five British Columbia mines will be the same in 1951 as in 1950, applying the new formula as contained in this measure those five mines will receive $71,000 additional in cost-aid payments. The amendment we plan to propose in committee stage will give further cost aid to these mines. It is expected that the additional cost aid will compensate, if not fully at least to a large extent, for the reduction in the exchange premium. If the cost of production increases the amount of cost aid payments will likewise increase.
Hon. members will recall that when Bill No. 194 was introduced reference was made to the fact that smaller total payments were made to the mines in Canada in 1950 under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act than in 1949. Payments in 1949 amounted to $12,500,000 on 3,614,000 ounces of gold production eligible for assistance. In 1950 the assistance is estimated at $9,200,000 on 3,874,523 assistance ounces. The explanation for the decrease in payments is due to the fact that the Canadian dollar was devalued in relation to the United States dollar and the $3.50 per assistance ounce was deducted from the assistance paid on all ounces eligible for assistance. In 1950 the exchange premium received by the gold mines amounted to about $11,500,000. Thus in that year the benefits received by the mines over and above the price of $35 an ounce was $20,700,000, including cost aid amounting to $9,200,000. In 1949 the exchange premium received by the gold mines amounted to $3,100,000. Thus in 1949 the benefits received by the mines over and above the price of $35 an ounce was $15,600,000, including cost aid of $12,500,000.
It should be remembered in making this comparison that gold production was increasing, so that production from lode and placer mines eligible for assistance was 236,000 ounces greater in 1950 than in 1949. It should be remembered also that during this period costf were rising and the formula under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act is designed to give greater aid with higher costs. On the same production and same costs in 1951 as in 1950 it is expected that the amount of assistance that will be paid under the measure now before the house will be $10,500,000. If, as in 1950, a gold production of 3,850,000 ounces is eligible for assistance, the amount of premium at a discount 80709-2701
Gold Mining
of 6 per cent for the Canadian dollar in relation to the United States dollar will be about $8,085,000. Thus in addition to the $35 an ounce the gold mines are expected to receive from assistance and the dollar premium a total of $18,585,000 in 1951. Thus the amount that will be received by the gold mines under the conditions outlined above will be approximately $2,100,000 less in 1951 than in 1950, but will exceed the 1949 figures by approximately $2 million.
The amendment which we propose to introduce in committee is designed to increase cost-aid payments to the mines by further substantial amounts. Some hon. members drew the conclusion that because the number of mines receiving assistance decreased last year, there must have been a number of companies going out of existence. What was actually happening was something very different. Following the devaluation of the Canadian dollar on September 20, 1949, the gold mines received $38.50 per fine ounce of gold produced and sold to the Royal Canadian Mint. In the months of 1949 after devaluation the gold mines received not only the benefit from devaluation but also the full amount of cost-aid. By the amendments of December 10, 1949, the amount of cost-aid was reduced to the extent of $3.50 per ounce by changing the cost-aid formula rate from cost minus eighteen to cost minus twenty-five. This eliminated from emergency assistance benefits mines whose costs per ounce were between $18 and $25. What these mines lost by cost-aid was offset by the increased exchange premium. Although not an exactly technically correct description of the method adopted, this is the practical effect of what has been done.
Accordingly, when the hon. member for Eglinton stated that the total number of mines being assisted was dropping from 111 in 1948 to 95 in 1949 and to 75 in 1950, the adjustment I have just described accounts for the non-appearance of several mines on the list of those receiving emergency aid. But the explanation of the chief discrepancy in the totals given of mines being assisted is that the hon. member was quoting totals appearing in the 1950 annual report on the administration of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. These totals were incomplete because the necessary audits were delayed in the case of certain applications, especially in regard to placer mining companies in northern British Columbia and the Yukon.
Reference to the 1951 annual report shows that instead of a decrease in the number of mines assisted, the total in 1948 of 117 was increased to 121 in 1949. The total given for 1950, namely 83, is of course not a complete

Gold Mining
figure but there is no reason to suppose that the 1950 total will not be as high as that of 1949, less probably three or four mines. The aim of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act that this bill amends was, as the name implies, to assist the gold mines during an emergency period, and it is generally admitted that the act has operated successfully to accomplish this purpose. It is believed that the revision now being presented will accomplish a similar purpose.

their number would be legion. I feel certain that if all restrictions on the sale of gold were removed we would have no difficulty in selling all our production at a price at least $10 over the present statutory price, and probably a great deal higher at the present time.
Refuting the third item of this article, the costs of putting gold into marketable form are not excessive. They run to a maximum of about 30 cents an ounce. The mint charges for this service are from three to ten cents an ounce, and they are making a reasonable charge. They have a sliding scale depending upon the fineness of the gold. On top of this, the Department of Finance collects a handling charge of 20 cents an ounce. The costs of over $2 per ounce, which the South Africans are forced to pay, are caused entirely by the fantastic regulations of the international monetary fund.
The procedure is as follows: Refined gold is produced from South African ore in the refinery in that country. This bullion is then adulterated down to 22 carats by the addition of an alloy. The so-called commercial gold is then shipped to the purchaser who has to manufacture it into objects of art, which generally take the form of easily poured little golden statues, and which are shipped out of the country to non-members of the international monetary fund where it is then rerefined to produce bullion and coins. Naturally, therefore, the cost of first refining the gold, second adulterating it down to 22 carats, third casting it into objects of art and shipping these to non-member countries, and fourth re-refining them into bullion . is an expensive operation. The entire cost of this, which is somewhere in the nature of $2 an ounce, is directly due to the ridiculous regulations of the international monetary fund. How much more profitable this market would be if South Africa could obtain this extra $2 an ounce is obvious. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this regulation has been deliberately made in order to make the South African operation as unprofitable as possible.
The fourth point in rebuttal is the substantial sales actually being made in increasing volume by South Africa. These figures I have already quoted. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, on these figures the operation of this extremely restricted market has been most profitable to South Africa and, judging from the latest figures, there has been a profit of over $534,000 in the last quarter. In the last available quarterly statement it appears that this market will be very much more profitable to her in the year to come. With regard to the expense and the establishment of a free market, I am convinced that 
an exchange mechanism could be established for buying and selling bullion similar to the bullion markets which existed before the first war, and that an extraordinarily handsome profit could be made by the brokers if they charged a tenth of 1 per cent commission. Probably it could be done for a great deal less, and I am certain the mining industry would be prepared to establish such a market without cost to anyone.
As a matter of fact I have been told that that is so, and certainly the gold mines of Ontario and the mines generally would be prepared to establish a bullion market similar to the one established in London, and would operate it without cost whatsoever. The device would be the establishment of a non-profit corporation, which is a familiar financial device.
The plight of the gold mines is well known. It can, however, be stated in quite simple terms. The cost of producing a unit of gold has gone up 68 per cent since before the war, and is steadily increasing. The price received is actually less now than obtained in 1939. What other product, whether raw or manufactured, could be sold today at prewar prices without the producer going bankrupt? The gold mining industry, in simple terms, is going bankrupt.
Here are the facts. In 1940 the industry made a net profit of $55 million. These figures are from the Canada Year Book. In 1947 this had been cut to $6 million after taxes, and half of this came from investment income. In 1950, without investment income, the industry made no profit, and today it is operating at a loss. I should like to mention that for the first time in our history mineral production in Canada passed the billion mark, and actually was, according to the latest D.B.S. estimate, more than 1,041 million. Of this gold was the largest single item, amounting to approximately 16 per cent. The importance of this industry cannot be overestimated, and despite the fact that our production increased last year the facts are plain for anyone to see. You cannot run an industry unless you are making profits. Unfortunately all of us know many enterprises that have had a big turnover and yet have gone bankrupt.
The effect of the bill is that the people of Canada have to pay through this subsidy approximately $12 million this year in order that the government may sell Canadian gold to the United States treasury at a price below that obtainable in the world market, and by so doing make a present to the United States of not only the subsidy but also the difference between the price we could obtain

on the free market for all our gold production and the sum obtained at the statutory price of $35 an ounce imposed on us by the Bretton Woods agreement. In other words, the Canadian people are bonusing the American people by $5 to $10 an ounce on nearly 4 million ounces or, conservatively, $25 million to $30 million this year, assuming a mean differential of only $7.50 per ounce.
Another question enters here. Today we are mining the rich ores of the mines. If this chamber could be considered an ore body, we are merely taking out the rich ore in the centre strip between the two lines of desks, leaving the great mass to the walls of the chamber untouched. That is a scandalous destruction of natural resources, because once the rich ore has been taken from a mine the low grade ore can never be recovered. Were we able to mine the ore bodies to their full width I am certain that the 4 million ounces, more or less, that we presently produce could be increased by at least 50 per cent within a period of three or four years. Given a production of 6 million ounces or the figure of 7 million ounces which has been mentioned to me, at the free market price of approximately $50 an ounce we are losing from $350 million to $400 million a year. We are jeopardizing an industry capable of producing that amount of new wealth every year. We are jeopardizing an industry that in those circumstances would cost the Canadian taxpayers nothing, an industry that above all others would help us in our adverse international balance of payments. We are doing that because of our adherence to the theories of the international monetary fund.
Not only are we doing this but, because our gold industry is operating at far below its productive capacity if the free market price were obtainable, we are losing the opportunity of selling much more of the prime product of our international trade. Today our unfavourable balance of payments with the United States is probably running at the rate of something over $400 million a year, and we cannot afford to lose any market. The free market price for gold in coin form is between $50 and $55 an ounce in Paris this week. I use Paris as being the best known and most steadily quoted rates. The average for the past year in coin form has fluctuated only some $7 an ounce or in the range of $47 to $54 an ounce in terms of United States dollars. Here I emphasize that the dollars quoted are United States dollars. The value of gold as against paper standards on the free market in Paris places the United States dollar at a discount of between 40 and 50 per cent in terms of gold. That is approximately what it has been depreciated to in purchasing
Gold Mining
power. Bar gold and raw bullion are quoted somewhat lower because the form they are in is not so convenient or acceptable to buyers. In this connection, England recently minted Sovereigns and, I believe, gold thalers, a coin acceptable in the Near East. Italy has also minted gold coins, and probably many other countries have wisely done so. If a consumer wants goods in a certain form and will pay for them it seems to me only good marketing practice to let him have them. Actually one can expect that if a free market were established in Canada the difference between the price of gold in coin form and the price in bar form would decrease until it almost disappeared. For the sake of convenience the gold coin will probably always sell for slightly more per ounce than the gold bar. Naturally bullion fineness of 24 carats is essential in all sales. Bullion is bullion, not 22 carats industrial gold or tubes of 80 per cent placer gold dust. Bullion is what is wanted on a free gold market; nothing else should be recognized or sold.
The value of gold to the economy of Canada has been questioned by the Social Credit party. As this party is from Alberta and Alberta quite rightly has pinned its faith on the oil industry, I think it would be interesting to hear what the leaders of the oil industry think about the gold industry. Last September when the provincial ministers of mines met in Victoria they were addressed by Mr. Auxier, president of the natural gas and petroleum association, which is the spokesman for that industry. In discussing the magnificent future he stated:
By the end of 1952 it is hoped that the Canadian oil industry would save Canada in foreign exchange $130 million annually or nearly as much as Canada's great gold industry.
That is what the spokesman of this industry had to say about gold mining even in its present depressed state. Were the gold industry to be given its head there is no doubt that for many years to come it would be a greater contributor to Canada's foreign exchange than the oil industry. Yet because of a slavish adherence to the instrument of a discredited economic theory, we are kicking the gold industry out of the window. The question which must be asked now is, is our membership in the international monetary fund worth the gold industry? I agree with hon. members of the Social Credit party that they were alone in sensing the danger of this international agency. I regret that I supported it; but originally it was to be an agency for the stabilization and freeing of world currencies. Actually the operations have been the absolute reverse; instead of freeing currencies and stabilizing
