them, nowhere in the world do you find freely exchangeable moneys except where there is a gold standard; and as I have pointed out before, the operation of the international monetary fund if anything has driven gold underground.
In resolutely opposing a free market the international monetary fund is doing the one thing that is destroying a return to the gold standard and fastening upon the world controlled currencies, restricted currencies, blocked currencies and several types of currency for every nation. Nothing is so holding up the recovery of Europe as the international frustration caused by currency control. Nothing so militates against us in Canada as our inability to freely exchange our currency with the nationals of other countries in payment for goods or services without either their government or our government interfering in the transaction. I say in all seriousness there is no agency today outside the communist world which has such a great potential for evil as the international monetary fund, and I am convinced that unless and until we withdraw from membership in that hydra-headed monster, the brain child of the Keynesian theorists, neither we nor the rest of the world with whom we wish to trade will recover. This device has been the supreme instrument for placing international trade in a strait-jacket. Unfortunately it has now become the instrument of policy of the United States treasury, and as such is undoing a great deal of the good of the Marshall plan. Having been in Europe for three months this year I can testify that nowhere did I see free currency. Everywhere there are restrictions between countries: national bank . restrictions, currency restrictions, restrictions on export sales, restrictions on imports so that the recovery of Europe is being delayed. The efforts of the magnificent Marshall plan were being frustrated and jeopardized because there was no adequate, free currency in Europe. I believe in all seriousness that a freely interchangeable currency is an absolute necessity for world recovery.
In this regard, I should like to quote from a speech made by O. Glen Saxon, professor of economics at Yale University, speaking before the thirty-first annual convention of the national association of mutual savings banks on May 7 of this year. In discussing the evils of the present economic theorists in the United States government, he stated that they had: (1) Devalued the dollar forty-one per cent in terms of gold; (2) partially remonetized silver further to dilute the money supply; (3) operated on an unbalanced

budget for twelve years; (4) repudiated the gold clause in government bonds and outlawed the gold clause in both past and future contracts, private and governmental; (5) made all United States money irredeemable in gold, except at the discretion of the treasury, and subject to progressive partial and possible total repudiation through inflation; (6) established arbitrary and artificially high values for foreign currencies; and, lastly, drained away the gold reserves of foreign nations and forced them to managed currencies, and created a monopoly of gold in the United States.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is this that is destroying world trade. Gold has been and always will be the lubricating medium on which the machinery of world trade operates. Until gold comes out of hoarding at Fort Knox and from private hoards throughout the world, it cannot fulfil this essential function. Therefore, it is imperative that we do everything to start gold flowing in the veins of international trade once more. Freeing it from all restrictions is the surest way to do this.

wish to make our position in connection with this bill quite clear. It appears to us that from the days when men worshipped the golden calf mankind has been inclined to be hypnotized by gold. I find that on page 1686 of Hansard for April 6, 1951, the member for Cochrane states:
I have an appeal to make at the present time, first of all to the national treasury, asking them to use all their influence to assist the gold mines, because the yardstick of gold must of necessity be maintained, . . .
We cannot agree in any sense with that position as advocated by the member for Cochrane. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in a few words I want to define our point of view concerning what wealth and money is, and our attitude towards the gold standard.
In our opinion wealth is something that sustains life or contributes to the well-being of society. A piece of bread, a bin of coal, a lovely flower, all contribute to life. Gold in the vaults at Ottawa, a bank note or a silver coin do not do this until they are exchanged for something else that is real wealth. We cannot eat money, nor can we drink it. It ministers to life only when it is exchanged for something else. The commodities which do sustain life are real wealth, and these are produced for us by the primary producers, the tillers of the soil; those who go down to the sea in ships; the lumbermen; the miners; and those who in a secondary way further the process of production or give services that make these products available to mankind. Now, Mr. Speaker, that is our definition of real wealth as opposed to the conception that looks upon gold as real wealth, and the real basis upon which currency and credit should be issued in this country. We believe that money is the financial wheel of our civilization carrying the accumulated labour receipts from one person to another and from one corner of the earth to another, even from one generation to another. Remember that it is the commodities that are important, not the wheel that circulates them; for it is through the commodities that our means of livelihood comes. For an individual to hoard gold, as money, is no more sensible than it is for a man to hoard wheels, in our opinion. Money is but a wheel in the financial world, and no amount of gold in the nations' treasuries can bring prosperity unless it is used to move commodities.
Just a brief word with regard to the gold standard. To many in this house the gold standard is almost sacred. We have been told that we must not meddle with this bulwark else the whole fabric of civilization will come tumbling about our ears. Some leaders, with an almost benediction hush in

Gold Mining
their voices, have informed Canadians from time to time that the country's honour was at stake and that the present international financial arrangements must not be molested, regardless of the fact that Canada has long since announced that no citizen would be paid gold in return for its currency, but that it was to be kept for the manipulations of the international bankers. We all know, Mr. Speaker, that so far as our internal currency is concerned, it is not in any sense of the word based on gold.
I cannot emphasize too strongly the fact that we in this group believe that man's labour on the earth is the only source of wealth and that gold has nothing to do with it; that our currency and credit have real value and that, to work effectively, must be based on the production of those who produce in this country and not upon the production of gold as in the past. We admit that the Bretton Woods agreement is an attempt to bring some stability to this artificial measure of value in the world, to bring some order out of chaos. The agreement indicates that even international bankers realize the necessity for some measure of planning. I should like to bring that fact to the attention of some of my friends to the right who were rather critical of the members of this group when they emphasized the fact that if we are going to have some order in international affairs and in our domestic economic affairs it is necessary to do some planning. Even international bankers have found it necessary to do some planning in order to try to bring order out of chaos in the establishment of the international monetary fund.

I know that the trade unions and the managements concerned say that Canada should not be restrained to $35 an ounce by the international monetary fund. I think the government should give serious copsideration to these representations.
In addition to that, we have the attitudes of governments towards the gold standard. I just want to give an illustration, for the benefit of my friend the hon. member for Cariboo. When governments come to think in terms of real value and real wealth, we find that they do not talk in terms of gold. Quite recently there was a hearing in the United States in connection with the application of the United States government for the building of a dam at Libby on the Kootenay river, which would flood a certain portion of the constituency of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne). The matter was brought before the international joint commission, for the members to hear of the circumstances. What do I read? The government of British Columbia gave serious consideration as to what the form of payment should take in compensation for this damage to Canadian territory. To support my argument that governments know what

real value is-that it is not gold, not currency, not money-I will quote from the brief of the government of British Columbia when considering compensation in connection with the application to build that dam. It reads as follows:
Because of the difficulties inherent in the fluctuating value of the dollar and the varying exchange rate, the province submits that the final settlement shall be in terms of an amount of electrical energy delivered at the international border at specified points for use in the province of British Columbia.
It is evident that the province of British Columbia knows what real value is; industrial power delivered to British Columbia can only be of increasing value throughout the years, and they were not willing to accept $1 million, $2 million, or $3 million in compensation for this damage and for the use of this water.
Then again I find that the East Kootenay Power Company Limited make a similar representation. I quote from their representation as follows:
It is submitted that a loss of this magnitude requires compensation to a like degree, and in a form not subject to the vagaries of rates of exchange or purchasing power of currencies.
They believe in the delivery of electrical energy. Again they are indicating their belief in what is real wealth, namely electrical power, not fluctuating currencies, gold or things of that sort.
Then the British Columbia Electric Company Limited made their representation:
That the logical way to compensate British Columbia for the economic loss which it will suffer from the flooding of the Kootenay valley is to arrange for a block of power from the Libby project to be set aside for the government of British Columbia.
That indicates the attitude of governments and of large corporations when they are considering what is real wealth. They know that human energy, human skills and ability, industrial power and natural resources are the bases of all real wealth today; and they are asking for industrial power in compensation for damage done to Canadian territory. They did not ask for a gold brick or for payment in dollars. They know what is real value.
In passing, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I noticed the other day in the Nelson Daily News of May 16, a daily published in my constituency, a headline which reads: "Money market may curb B.C. plans. Cities, school boards face same difficulties. $40 million credit to be sought in east or United States by Anscomb, deputy". The article goes on to say:
Mr. Anscomb will leave for the east shortly with his deputy, J. V. Fisher, to attempt to borrow the funds required for British Columbia's planned capital works.

To go to New York to borrow that money which will be based on British Columbia natural resources, British Columbia labour and British Columbia industrial power is something that we in this group do not agree with. We in this group say it would be far better to take this gold, keep it in Canada if you want to issue your credit and currency on it and not go to New York to borrow money. Better still to issue loans to our provinces, to our municipalities and to our school boards, based on the natural resources, the industrial production and the labour power of the province. There is no necessity to go to the United States, because these people lend that money exactly on that security. We in this group cannot see why this government cannot use the machinery of government, the Bank of Canada, to finance sound capital investment by the provinces and by the dominion government itself.
We find that representations have been made to the government for gold mining assistance. Representations have been made through the labour organizations directly concerned with the gold mining industry. As I said before, the labour organizations advocate a free market for gold. I do ask the government to give serious consideration to these representations.
The government has had representations from the gold mining industry, from the Canadian Metal Mining Association, the British Columbia Mining Association and representatives of municipalities. I had the pleasure of being with the representatives of some northern Ontario and Quebec municipalities when they made representations to two or three members of the government. I was impressed indeed with the presentation made by a lady reeve, from one of the northern municipalities. She made a very capable and effective presentation of the case for these municipalities.
On top of that, the government of British Columbia has indicated its position. The legislature of British Columbia unanimously adopted a resolution urging continuation of assistance to the gold mining industry under present circumstances.
We in this group support this bill because we must give human, practical, and immediate consideration to the needs of 23,000 miners and to 125,000 Canadians who are directly affected at this time by the gold mining industry. Second, we support this bill because the present condition is caused by international and government action.
' Third, we believe the miners are entitled to fair wages and satisfactory housing, and that it is necessary to protect the life savings

Gold Mining
of many of those people in homes, small businesses and service in the communities surrounding the mines affected.
Fourth, we believe it is necessary to protect the large public investment, federal, provincial and municipal in the communities and areas surrounding the gold mining districts.
Fifth, under the present economic system we in Canada receive goods in exchange for gold sold to the United States. In our opinion, the world of the future will not use labour to take gold from one hole and place it in another in order to protect a gold standard. But in the meantime we must be realistic, for in return for our gold we get commodities and goods that we require.
I have read the report of the Gold Mining Assistance Act, and I have read several of the speeches made, and I may make an observation or two in committee. I noted in reading that report that several large companies operate very profitable enterprises; that is, several very large and very profitable enterprises are receiving assistance for the operation of a mine or two, the operation of a iron-profitable gold mine or two.
First, when considering assistance under this act, Mr. Speaker, the total operations of any corporation should receive consideration. If the company has diversified its operations so that it is carrying on large operations in several spheres, the very fact that it operates a relatively small gold mining operation at a loss should not be considered. I think the total position of the company concerned, shall I say, should be considered when dealing with a question of assistance to these companies.
I do not intend to say very much more, Mr. Speaker, but I may ask a few questions when the bill is in committee. We in this group are particularly concerned about the standard of wages received by the employees of the gold mining industry. To date gold miners have been paid lower wages than miners in other hard-rock mines. The owners have constantly maintained that they could not afford to pay higher wages.
The minister when speaking said that the assistance provided in the bill would enable the companies to make a legitimate profit. According to my understanding of the word "legitimate" it means a lawful or regular profit. In view of the word "legitimate" meaning a lawful or regular profit, and the large lawful profits being made by many companies today, the word could possibly mean that some of these companies would make a very large profit, because the word legitimate simply means a lawful or regular
[Mr. Herridge.l
profit. We maintain that when companies are receiving this assistance from the government the first claim on the production and the first claim on this assistance should be a satisfactory standard of wages in relationship to the mining industry as a whole, and proper working conditions. We urge that in granting these subsidies the government should insist as a first qualification for assistance that the miners in the industry receive the standard wages and the same working conditions as miners in other hard-rock mines.
In conclusion, I again state that we support this measure as a necessary temporary expedient because it involves the livelihood of 23,000 miners and the welfare of 120,000 Canadians, and because of the large public and private investments in mining, communities and the surrounding areas; but we do realize that this is no final solution. It is a purely temporary measure, that in effect indicates the inconsistencies and contradictions of our present economic system.

I mention that fact because we should be a little more consistent in this house on the question of subsidies, and deal with them in a fairer manner.
However, in spite of that fact, I say we support this subsidy; but I would point out that as war or fear of war may expand the demand for goods in this country I think that the gold miners could probably be better

employed elsewhere because already I understand there is developing a shortage of miners, and also I understand that already there is looming a shortage of mining engineers. I say that because after all monetary gold does not provide any essential service. As a matter of fact, at all times when it has been urgent that the production of the country be increased as rapidly as possible we have been forced off the gold basis. We have found that we could not bring about a rapid increase in our production as long as we were on the gold basis. That is what happened in 1940 and we are still off the gold basis.
The hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) and other members of the Conservative party have referred to the part played by gold in balancing our trade with other nations. That is true, and it has been especially true so long as our trade followed what was called the triangular pattern. This pattern was referred to often by the former minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, who pointed out that we had a large favourable balance of trade with the sterling areas and a large unfavourable balance of trade with the United States and therefore we would have to insist that countries in the sterling areas pay their deficits in either United States dollars or gold in order that we might make up our deficit with the United States.
I have often wondered why we should consider it the responsibility of nations in Europe to make up our unbalance of trade with the United States. Unfortunately, as a result of that policy, we have found nations in Europe curtailing their imports from this country in order to avoid having a deficit with us and being under the obligation to hand over United States dollars or gold in order to balance their payments.
It is a good thing for the country that today we have a Minister of Trade and Commerce who apparently realizes the true functions of trade. Last year the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) pointed out that the only way to overcome the difficulties that were encountered in that triangular form of trade was to increase our sales to the United States and increase our purchases from the sterling area. As a result of that attitude we find today that we practically have a balanced trade with Europe instead of a large favourable balance of trade, and we are doing everything we can to balance our trade with the United States by increasing exports.
In order to make a maximum contribution toward supplying the needs of backward nations and for the purposes of building up defences, I think the members of the United Nations should do everything in their power
Gold Mining
to discourage the production of what might be termed useless goods. It will be recalled that that was the policy during world war II. When it became essential during world war II that we increase the production of munitions and food we curtailed the production of gold. When you realize the situation in the world today it is quite evident that there is a great need for expansion in the production of food to feed the starving people in many countries. After all, we cannot feed gold to those people. I should like to refer to the report of the director general of FAO for 1949-50 and I quote from page one as follows:
There is far too little food for the world's hungry mouths, and the yearly increase in production is not enough to keep pace with the increase in the number of human beings. A third of the world's people enjoy health, wealth and wellbeing to a comparatively high degree; the other two-thirds live on intimate terms with poverty, hunger, disease, illiteracy and premature death. Even where production is most highly developed, farmers are subject to the vagaries of markets to such an extent that they run heavy risks by planning ahead for abundance. These bitter contrasts break out in discontent and rebellion because -and this is the most significant development of our time-every day more people realize that such conditions are no longer necessary. Modern advances in science and technology make greatly increased well-being possible for all mankind, and there is no insurmountable barrier to that achievement.
When you have that sort of situation in the world where not enough food is being produced to meet the needs of the people I think it is rather futile to suggest that you can stabilize world currencies by putting them on a gold basis. If you put currencies on a gold basis and at the same time have a shortage of food, will that gold prevent inflationary pressure in the demand for goods? Certainly it will make no difference whether that currency is on a gold basis or not unless there are goods to satisfy the demand created by that money. Therefore, the only way to avoid inflation, the only way to stabilize the currencies of the world, is to increase production so as to make sure that there will be a sufficient amount of goods and services to satisfy the demand created by the money in circulation.
When the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) spoke on the resolution stage he supported a free market for gold and gave South Africa as an example of the benefits that accrue to nations when they are able to sell some of their gold on that market. There are a number of reasons why I would oppose a free market for gold under the existing set-up, that is so long as our currency is valued in terms of gold under the international monetary fund.

Gold Mining
The first question I would ask is: Would the gold mine operators actually be better off if they were able to sell their gold in a free market than they would selling it under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act? I listened with interest to what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said. He stated that in his opinion the gold mine operators probably would not be any better off by selling their gold on a free market than they would under this act. I was interested in that because those views correspond closely with the views expressed by the Financial Post and the Financial News. I do not think anyone will suggest that either the Financial Post or the Financial News is opposed to the production of gold. I should like to quote from a statement which anpeared in the Financial Post of April 14, 1951, under the heading, "Free gold market not so profitable. Cost-aid returns seen just as great." This article by Gordon M. Grant reads:
Statisticians see several factors indicating the current $42 an ounce free market price for gold might prove illusory when it came to realizing the extra benefit on the entire Canadian output.
1.	The free market has not "steadily risen." It collapsed early in February, 1950-South Africa had to discontinue sales then-and only recovered the latter part of last year.
2.	Efforts to liquidate entire Canadian gold production at $42 an ounce could easily break the market, inspire increased selling by South Africa.
3.	Costs of putting gold into marketable form, and selling it, might run $3.20 an ounce or more- about half the "extra" gold mines might hope to secure. South Africa is reported to find it unprofitable to sell gold below $38.20 United States on the free market.
And again:
Early experience of South Africa gold mines with premium sales on the free market shows that returns were much less than the extra amount Canadian gold mines received under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.
And further down:
In recent months, it appears pretty definite that South Africa has been able to sell 40 per cent of her output on the free market-and perhaps at the $42 United States price per ounce. But averaged over her entire output, the extra revenue is only providing a gold yield of about $37.80 United States per ounce. From this figure must be deducted the expenses of fabrication and selling on the free market. These expenses are important because marketing costs on sale of gold to the Canadian mint are relatively negligible. Even with sale of 40 per cent of their output on the free market South African gold mines are probably no better off than Canadian gold mines under the set-up for 1951.
I shall not take the time to quote from the Financial News, but the article in that publication was exactly the same as the argument put forward by the Financial Post. There is another point I should like to raise. Under

the international monetary fund gold is used as the yardstick and currencies are valued in terms of gold. That being the case, would it be wise to make gold subject to the vagaries of international gamblers and financiers? It seems to me that you can hardly expect to stabilize currency by using gold as a standard of value if it is subject to wild fluctuations in such markets as Hong Kong, Bombay and other hot spots of the world. On the other hand, I would have absolutely no objection to a free market for gold provided first of all that it was divorced entirely from our monetary system. On that basis I would be prepared to support a free market, but would those people who are today asking for a free market be willing to accept it on that basis? I would say they would be most bitterly opposed to a free market for gold if gold was divorced from the monetary system. They realize that a part of the prestige that gold has today is the fact that it is used as a yardstick for our currency. Furthermore they want to have that prestige for gold apparently without accepting the responsibility that goes with it, the responsibility of stabilizing the price of gold.
Under the international monetary fund, which has been referred to during this debate, gold is the only commodity which nations can use as of right to liquidate their external trade deficits. That being the case, would it be wise to allow the price of gold to be dominated by such spots as Hong Kong, Bombay or any other spot in the world today where there is fear and uncertainty? In such places we find people trying to change their worldly assets into the form of gold so that they can pack it up and take it out of the country. One wonders how long a market of that kind could last. Moreover, where would they get the currency with which to buy our gold, and would the currency thus obtained be of any use for the purpose of balancing our trade with the United States, which is the main purpose of gold today in so far as Canada is concerned?
When the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) spoke he mentioned that I did not oppose section 8 of article IV of the international monetary fund. Section 8 reads:
The gold value of the fund's assets shall be maintained notwithstanding changes in the par or foreign exchange value of the currency of any member.
It is true that when the bill concerning the monetary fund was before the standing committee on banking and commerce I did not oppose that section for the obvious reason that I had bitterly opposed sections 1 to 6. Once sections 1 to 6 had been carried it was

obvious that section 8 was required to carry out the purpose of sections 1 to 6. Section 1 reads:
The par value of the currency of each member shall be expressed in terms of gold as a common denominator or in terms of the United States dollar of the weight and fineness in effect on July 1, 1944.
In other words, we opposed gold being used as a yardstick for the currencies of the world. We opposed the idea of all currencies of all member nations being valued in terms of gold. Furthermore, we opposed a subsequent section which made it impossible for a nation to change the value of its currency to a greater degree than 10 per cent without the permission of the fund. Sections 1 to 6 carried; and, once they had been carried, obviously section 8 was necessary to implement those sections. But I would point out that article IV was not the main article that we opposed in the Bretton Woods agreement. The chief reason we opposed the Bretton Woods agreement was that gold is the only commodity a creditor nation is obliged to accept in payment of debts owing to it.
In other words, we criticized the monetary fund because it gave the creditor nations the right to demand payment in gold for their balances held abroad, instead of placing upon them the obligation to accept payment in the only commodity with which most nations could pay, goods and services. I should like to refer to what I said at that time because the hon. member for Cochrane seemed to be a little bit confused and seemed to think that we were supporting gold as the basis. At page 131 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the standing committee on banking and commerce of December 13, 1945, I had this to say with respect to Bill No. 238:
It is interesting to note under this agreement that gold will be the only commodity in the world that a creditor nation is obliged to accept in payment of its debt. I realize it is not done directly. It is done via the fund. That makes no difference, and the witness agreed with me, no substantial difference. What is bound to be the result of that situation? It is all very well to call it a breathing spell, but they will not be able to breathe very long under a proposal of that kind, because when you realize the size of nations' unbalances of trade and the fact that they can only borrow up to 25 per cent of their quota in any one year they will not even be able to obtain enough currency from the fund to pay off the unbalance of trade. So it will not in reality prove a breathing spell. The situation that will face a debtor nation will be this. They will either have to cut down their standard of living to the very minimum, cut off imports, which will be contrary to the purpose of the fund, because the purpose is supposed to be to expand trade, and if a nation as a result of this is forced to cut down imports and reduce its standard of living to the minimum it would be directly contrary to the purpose of the fund. Instead of the fund helping to bring about an expansion of trade
Gold Mining
it will be helping to develop economic nationalism, the very thing it is supposed to prevent. I do charge that under this act that is exactly what will happen . . .
Is that not exactly what happened with regard to Europe? They found that they suffered from unfavourable balances of trade with the dollar countries and therefore they placed restrictions upon imports of goods from the dollar area. They cut down their standard of living to the minimum and adopted a very strong form of economic nationalism within the sterling area. I am not going to try to take any credit for the fact that we foresaw what was bound to happen at that time because it was so obvious that under the international monetary fund that was bound to be the consequence of such. a policy. At that time we advocated an alternative, and again I should like to refer to page 131 where I said:
What we want in the act mainly is a provision that a debtor nation in order to pay for its imports shall be recognized as paying for them when they establish a credit within their country in favour of a creditor nation and that that credit can be used to buy anything purchased within that country. Then if the creditor nation is not willing to accept goods from a nation with which it has a credit if it desires to trade on a multilateral basis it may trade the credit established on that basis for the credit of another country on a multilateral basis. So I say if the great industrialized nations are really sincere in this matter they should have shown it at this time and been willing to have an article to that effect put in the Bretton Woods agreement.
When we insisted time and again that an article of that kind should be put in the Bretton Woods agreement to ensure that the debtor nations would be in a position to pay off their debts by shipment of goods we were told that was a question of trade agreements, that it did not come within the confines of the international monetary fund, that it would be taken care of later on by some form of international trade organization. What happened when the international trade organization was set up? We found that it still further aggravated the situation because it introduced the policy that is often referred to as a policy of non-discrimination.
We in, this group are therefore opposed to the currency of this nation or, if we had the power, the currencies of any nation, being valued in terms of gold because the real value of a nation's currency depends upon the amount of goods and services that that currency will buy, and no amount of gold will change that. If you do not have the goods and services within the country, then no matter how much gold you have unless you can exchange it for goods that currency will become worthless because there will not be any goods for it to buy. If you had an island

Gold Mining
in the middle of the ocean with stocks of gold and no goods, the currency of that island would be absolutely useless. The only thing that makes a currency of value, as I say, is the goods and services that can be bought with it.
We have heard members of the Conservative party, particularly the hon. member for York West, advocating a return to the gold standard. Thank goodness the people of Canada will never tolerate the restoration of the automatic features of the gold standard, because we are not prepared to permit our people to be disciplined in that way. What does that mean? It would mean that any time our standard of living got a little higher than that of other nations and the prices of goods in this country rose above the prices in other nations so they were not buying our goods freely, gold would flow from this country to other nations and as a result currency would be withdrawn from circulation, unemployment would increase, production would go down and goods would pile up. After a while, of course, the presumption is that the process would be reversed; the prices of goods would fall, gold would come flowing back and the situation would be restored. The people of this country are not prepared to see men unemployed while at the same time we have great resources to be developed, resources which if developed can satisfy the needs of all the people of this country.
However, as I have already said, as long as we are members of the international monetary fund and therefore encouraging the production of gold, I believe legislation such as this is justified temporarily. We in this group do believe, however, that at the very earliest opportunity the articles of the international monetary fund should be thoroughly overhauled and gold displaced as the yardstick, and that the currencies of the world should be supported by a goods basis instead. I remember a westerner once coming to Ottawa and advocating that our currency be tied to wheat instead of gold. To those who feel we must have our currency tied to one commodity instead of to a price level I say it would be far more reasonable and logical to have wheat as the basis for our currency than gold, because wheat is of great use in the world. It would mean that if our currency were tied to wheat, any nation in the world obtaining our currency would know it could be exchanged for wheat, which is so urgently needed in every part of the world today. Starving nations would be glad to get our wheat, whereas gold is of little use to them unless they can turn around and exchange it immediately 
for goods. So if we have to tie our currency to one commodity I say wheat would be far more sensible, because we always have plenty of wheat and any time our currency got into the hands of another nation they could redeem it in this country for wheat.
As I listened to the hon. member for York West I could not help thinking how many forms of bugs we have in the human race. We have the gold bugs, who want to develop gold. We have the jitterbugs who want to develop the jitters. We have the firebugs, who want to develop fires; and we have other people who are just plain bugs. If you think too much about gold you may develop that attitude.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill was given first reading in this house on April 6, two and a half months ago. Many of us hoped that in the interval the government would evolve some new policy or some amendment which would really meet the situation. While a slight amendment has been indicated by the minister, we must view the situation as one for which the government has failed to propose an adequate remedy. While of course the bill will be approved, since it is a good deal better than nothing, nevertheless it seems to me to be open to four fundamental criticisms. In the first place, it is inadequate in the provision it makes for the gold industry. In the second place, it is only temporary, just a makeshift and stopgap. In the third place, by its very nature it is necessarily discriminatory. In the fourth place, it is only an artificial remedy. The amendment simply represents more tinkering with that artificial, inadequate remedy. In brief, I think we must have either a free market or a realistic and adequate price for gold.
Some of the statements offered in the house this evening concerning gold have been a little surprising. In some of the speeches, if I may say so, there has been a want of appreciation of the part gold has played in the history of the world, in the history of trade and the history of currencies. Gold has always been the universally accepted medium of exchange throughout human history. Today no one can estimate the importance of gold to our economy or the economy of the world without due recognition of that fact. It is not simply a matter of the gold standard, though that has a bearing. It is a question of recognizing the part gold has had to play and still has to play in providing a means by which nations of the world may trade with one another and find something all will agree upon as a medium for settling their commodity

trading balances. All the world over gold has that peculiar and unique value and position. Today all countries, even Russia, seek gold, while the Kremlin is putting obstacles in the way of trade among the nations of the world.
Canada has a peculiar interest in this subject as a producer. When I hear hon. members belittling the place of gold in the world's economy I think they fail utterly to recognize the importance of gold production in our history, in the Canadian economy and in its good health.
At this late hour I am not going to indulge in quotations as to the importance of gold. When I spoke on April 6 I quoted what I thought were authoritative statements by persons such as Dr. Camsell, who have had a long connection and intimate experience with this subject. Gold played an invaluable part in preserving the economy of this country during the depression days. As much as any other industry in this country the gold industry pulled us through the worst of that depression experience.
Gold Mining
It would be well also to bear in mind that in Canada the ownership of gold mines is very widely distributed. It is not a case of concentrating wealth in the hands of the few. Gold shares, representing ownership of this industry, are widely distributed.
Gold has had a unique position and use in the history of this country also in providing the means of settling our commodity trading deficit with the United States. There has always been a market in that country for our gold production. During the years when our trading deficit with the United States was very high we were glad indeed to turn to our gold production as a means of meeting that deficit on commodity trading account. I have some figures, and to save time I should like to put them on the record if the house will permit me. They are taken from the government publication Foreign Trade, volume 9, page 993, of June 2, 1951.

Those figures take us to the end of the third month of 1951. The record for the fourth month of this year shows a deficit of $93 million on our trading account with the United States. This has been a continuous feature of our history.
The dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin of April 24 notes that on our current account with all nations in 1950 we had an excess of all types of imports over all types of exports of $316 million. It comments that these adverse trends were only slightly offset by a rise from $139 million to $163 million in gold available for export. This recalls to the minds of all who study this problem that gold is one commodity to which we have always been able to turn to help meet this chronic deficit of our commodity trading account with the United States.
Now, the gold mining industry has sustained great areas of this country, particularly in the two old provinces of Ontario and Quebec, but not confined to those provinces. It has been an important factor in the economic life of Manitoba and British Columbia. The needs of this industry today, and the way in which it has become a plaything of national and international policy, are reflected in the way in which some of these great mining camps, which were marked not long ago by flourishing and growing cities, are today presenting a picture of shrinkage and steady decay. No Canadian who has any appreciation of the sound elements of the economy of this country can sit back and contemplate with any degree of indifference or satisfaction the way in which the communities directly owing their economic life to the great mining camps of this country are suffering. We must open our eyes to this threatening situation, and the manner in which those areas have been

Gold Mining
suffering. If this industry is permitted to decay, no longer are these communities going to be great markets for the products of other industries. What is to become of the savings of the workmen in those areas represented by their investments in their homes? These are not vague possibilities. These are real dangers that are confronting these mining areas today, and the people who owe their livelihood to the health of this industry.
The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) on April 6 quite properly paid a tribute to the part played by gold in sustaining the search for and the production of base metals. With the critical shortage of some of these base metals today as the world scrambles for commodities essential for rearmament, we must not overlook or minimize the importance of gold as supporting the search for these base metals.
Now, sir, a crisis is rapidly developing in our gold mining industry in Canada. When I spoke on April 6 I made some reference to comments made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he spoke in Timmins prior to the last general election. I believe the best recent summary of the situation I have found appeared in the last issue of the Monetary Times, in an article written by Mr. E. C. Gould, the financial editor. He sums up the situation in two or three paragraphs which read as follows:
The truth of the matter is that at many Canadian gold mines, a greater part of the ore mined since 1946 has been taken from underground workings, completed and financed in prior years. Owing to an increase in costs and the resultant reduction in the volume of profitable ore, the development of a ton of new ore is now three to four times the 1939 cost. Based on the current price for gold, this situation makes it uneconomical for many mines to open up new levels and they are gradually depleting the ore developed in prior years with a shutdown in prospect unless early and substantial relief is forthcoming. As a result, the gold mining areas are becoming depressed and the former rich relation of the mining world can no longer meet the high cost of existence from the returns of a fixed income. So far have we departed from the "age of gold" that now "the lowly hen, must be laughing at the goose that laid the golden egg."
The plight of the gold industry was described by Prime Minister St. Laurent as early as June, 1949, in a way that left little hope for profitable speculation. "Many gold mines in Canada," he said, "now are just staggering along because they are being squeezed between the fixed price of gold, $35 per ounce, and the high cost of production per ounce of gold recovered . . . The grim shadow of mine shutdowns has been hanging over many gold mining properties."
That is a quotation from the speech which the Prime Minister made at Timmins during the election campaign in 1949. The article continues:
Since June, 1949, this gloomy picture has certainly not improved for costs have increased $3.75

per ounce and the rate of gold assistance has been reduced.
According to figures, based on profits published in the Bank of Canada statistical summary, the average total earnings per year, for the years 1946 to 1949, for 38 gold mines were less than 30 per cent of the average for the years 1938 to 1940. A comparable figure for 643 Canadian companies, representing all industries, is 180 per cent for the same periods. The ratio of gold mining profits, therefore, is one-sixth of the average of all Canadian industries when compared with the average for 1938 to 1940.
The following is a picture of the current situation in the Canadian gold mining industry, outlined by the president of one of Canada's more successful gold mines in an appeal for what he terms the "adjusting of gold to a sound price basis": "The number of gold mines in Canada is being steadily reduced as mines are forced to close down due to rapidly rising costs while the price received for gold is below the 1939 level. The increase in average operating costs since 1939 is equal to over $15 per ounce or 75 per cent. Since 1946, when the price of gold was reduced to $35 in Canada, costs have increased by about $9 per ounce, made up of increases in wages of about 50 per cent equal to $6 per ounce and in supply costs of over 50 per cent equal to $3 per ounce. The cost of developing a new mine, building a plant and bringing the mine into production on a basis of 500 tons per day has increased from approximately one million dollars in 1939 to a minimum of two million, five hundred thousand dollars in 1951, while the estimated profit per ton of ore is now only a small fraction of the 1939 figure."
This is a matter of concern to all Canadians.
The fundamental problem of the gold mining industry today is not lack of markets, it is the price. This problem is the result of price control. Here is one commodity that has been singled out above all others for the application of price control. That has been in effect now ever since-

speechtext:
But on a very different basis now, if you please; that is the very point of this objection. I think that is the fundamental fallacy of the government's approach to it. Gold has been singled out for price control under an international agreement to which this country is a signatory, and so far as we have been permitted to know the government has been content to accept that ceiling on a product which Canada produces in large quantities. When Canada submits to a ceiling price, Canada necessarily absorbs a loss. Again, it is not all Canada that is absorbing this loss. The government has not approached this problem the way they approached the problems created by price ceilings in some other important Canadian products. Here the government has been content, apart from the altogether inadequate assistance provided by the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, to see the gold mining

industry absorb these losses that are imposed upon it by a measure of price control on an international basis which the government of this country has supported. The result has been discrimination practised upon this industry, and a retarding of the growth of this industry; setbacks to this industry from which it will take a long time, and much more prosperous conditions, if it is ever to recover.
The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) took some satisfaction out of the fact that last year there was a slight increase in national production of gold over the year 1949. If he looks at the figures for the first three months of this year he will see that we are now showing a slight decrease in monthly production. I may attempt this prophecy also, Mr. Speaker: if the present measure, even with the indicated amendment, is all that this government has to offer to the gold-mining industry, we are going to see a continuation in the trend evidenced in the production figures for the first three months of this year. That is something that is fraught with serious dangers for the economy of Canada.
I must take issue with the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys with regard to some of the inferences which he has drawn from the report on the administration of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1951. In the year 1948,	117 gold-mining companies
received benefits under this act; in 1949 the number was 121; but in 1950 the number has dropped to 83, which is just two-thirds of the number in the previous year. What may we expect for 1951? Unless something is done to give help and hope to this gold-mining industry I may confidently venture the prediction that fewer gold-mining companies are going to receive assistance from this act.
Let us just look at the figures. In 1948 the government paid out through this act $10,500,000. I shall just give the round figures. In 1949 they paid out $12,500,000. But in 1950 the amount dropped to just a trifle over $7 million. This year the amount estimated was $9,200,000; the amendment contemplates another $900,000, or $10 million in round figures, an amount substantially below the figures of 1948 and 1949. In other words, while the needs of the industry have grown apace as costs have been soaring, the government contributes less in order to try to repair the damage the government policy has done to that industry deliberately, by following a policy of lopsided and discriminatory price control.
I spoke of rising costs. I think a study would repay hon. members of this house in
Gold Mining
order to see how costs have been rising in the gold-mining industry, and to see just how much more it costs today to produce an ounce of gold than it did five, ten or fifteen years ago. If I bad the time to do so, or were not concerned about wearying the house with statistics, I should like to put some figures on Hansard in that respect. I will just shortly give you a sample in passing, Mr. Speaker, of the kind of competition that the goldmining industry is up against. There are many miners engaged in the gold-mining industry who today are working at rates substantially below those prevailing in some of the other mining industries. How do you expect the gold-mining industry to compete for miners with some of the other industries like nickel, for instance, for which there is an ever-expanding market at an uncontrolled price? Here is a dispatch from Port Colborne, dated May 22, which reads as follows:
New agreement reached by the International Nickel Co. of Canada Ltd., and the International Union of Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers will mean wage increases of from 23 to 26 cents per hour plus a 40-hour week. The agreement affects 14,500 workers here and in Sudbury.
Then further down:
New wage rates will run from $1.53 to $1.88 per hour, except for partially incapacitated employees, who will receive $1.46.
The gold-mining industry cannot compete with wage rates like those as long as it is left to languish under this price control system imposed upon it by the government. Consequently men are driven away from the gold-mining industry into these other mining industries. But think of the hardship that imposes upon these people, in giving up their residence in areas where they have lived their lives, made their livelihood and invested their life savings in homes. They are now called upon to leave those areas, sell their homes at a sacrifice, and go to other areas in order to find work in mines which produce metals other than gold.
We in this house, Mr. Speaker, if I may say so, often fail adequately to realize the simple fact that an extremely narrow margin in costs or in price makes a world of difference with regard to turning what may be marketable ore into useless rock, or vice versa.
Proceeding as quickly as I can, Mr. Speaker, I come to the question of our national interests. As to the gold-mining industry, Canada's interest is all on the side of the producer; because our interests as consumers of gold are trifling as compared with the interests of Canada as a producer of gold. When we look at the government policy of discriminatory price control practised on this commodity, in which Canada's interest is altogether on the side of production, we must

Gold Mining
wonder, Mr. Speaker, that this commodity is chosen to be sacrificed on the altar of high government policy.
I would not be disposed to take a narrow view of this subject if, on international balance, Canada were receiving some quid pro quo in return for the sacrifice it is making of its interests as a gold producer, and provided that some attempt were made, as between our government and the gold producers of this country, to lift the burden of the sacrifice off the shoulders of that one industry. But where do we find some quid pro quo in this scale or in this international balance? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) can point to the need of international co-operation. Here is, on Canada's part, an exceedingly costly contribution to international co-operation. I think that the Canadian gold producer is entitled to ask for something in return for this contribution that is being exacted of him toward international co-operation or better international relations. Why should he be singled out, and why should his interests be sacrificed on this altar of international relations? We have heard nothing from the government to justify the singling out of the gold-mining industry for that unhappy role.
Looking back to 1945 when we entered the Bretton Woods agreement, I would point out that we then had a quite different world situation before us than this one we face now. One has only to look back at the preamble to the Bretton Woods agreement which in the light of the unhappy world conditions of 1951, reads today almost like a fairy story. Yet the gold-mining industry of this country, by government policy, tied to this international agreement, is made to suffer because the world has not been able to translate into actuality that pretty picture that we drew in 1945.
Let me now mention one or two facts of recent history. The international monetary fund, in its policy, has been largely under the domination of the United States, from the outset. The interest of the United States in the matter of gold is, on balance, fundamentally strongly on the side of the consumer. The United States has been over the years a vast net importer of gold. It is difficult to see how there can be a harmonization of the interests of Canada and the interests of the United States in a fund of that kind; it certainly cannot take place as long as United States interests as a gold-consuming country or a gold-importing country are to dominate the international monetary fund's policy.
Recently we have seen some indication of an attempt on the part of the international

monetary fund to influence policy in regard to the revaluation of the currencies of Europe. I have a press dispatch from Geneva, dated May 27:
The United Nations Economic Commission for Europe urged today an immediate and drastic revaluation of European currencies to turn the mounting tide of inflation.
But the international monetary fund within a week showed that they were opposed to it. This is a dispatch from London that appeared in a Canadian newspaper of June 4. I read a few sentences:
Considerable stimulus has been given to the controversy over the possibility or desirability of the revaluation of sterling by the recent declarations of the Economic Commission for Europe and the International Monetary Fund. Interest is added to their views by the fact that they are strongly opposed to each other.
The international monetary fund has expressed the opinion that no upward revaluation of sterling should be undertaken or contemplated until there has been a general relaxation of restrictions on international payments. The Economic Commission for Europe declares boldly in favour of revaluation, arguing that revision of exchange rates is one of the most effective means of fighting inflation.
But, sir, so far as we can see the policy of the international monetary fund is going to prevail.
In recent months, in fact over the past year, the United States has been obliged to export gold, largely owing to the increasing health of Britain's international trade, and Britain has been importing gold over the past year. The international financial news survey, a publication of the international monetary fund of May 11, says this in its opening paragraph:
Net gold sales by the United States to other countries amounted to $898 million in the first quarter of 1951, which corresponds to an annual rate of $3,590 million. This was a rise of about one-sixth above the already high fourth quarter of 1950.
The annual report of our own Canadian foreign exchange control board for the year 1950 reminds us on page 17 of this fact:
In order to meet the demand by Canadians substantial amounts of sterling were obtained by Canada from the United Kingdom in exchange for gold.
Gold has been going to the United Kingdom on account of Canada's trading relationships with her, too. Then, sir, in the Federal Reserve Bulletin of March, 1951, at page 257 in an article entitled: "The international movement of gold and dollars in 1950", one reads this paragraph:
Improvement in the gold and dollar positions abroad was widespread in 1950, as shown in the accompanying table and chart. Only a few countries, including Belgium, Norway, and Venezuela, failed to add to their holdings. Almost two-thirds of the over-all increase was concentrated in the

United Kingdom and Canada. These two countries, however, distributed their gains differently. The United Kingdom converted practically all its current dollar receipts (1-0 billion dollars) into gold, in addition to obtaining another estimated half billion dollars in gold from other sources. On the other hand, Canada's gold reserves increased by only $100 million in this period, while its dollar balances rose by over $500 million and were largely invested in United States government securities.
Continental countries participating in the European recovery program purchased about $380 million in gold from the United States during 1950 (of which about $200 million was included in monetary reserves) and added about 400 million to their dollar balances.
Now sir, in the face of that fact I submit to you that Canada has not been paying sufficient attention to gold, not even to her own gold supply, because if we look at the government publication, "The Canadian Balance of International Payments, 1950", at page 6 we will see some very startling figures. If I may put these figures on Hansard without reading them it would save time of the house.

I invite attention to the fact that during the year 1950 our gold holdings increased by only $100 million, while our holdings of United States dollars increased by over $500 million. Now, Mr. Speaker, we are not paying enough attention in this country, at least government policy is not paying enough attention, to the signs of the times and the way that the gold is being taken up by other countries, all these countries of Europe to which reference has been made; and we are laying up a store of United States dollars when under present conditions we might far better be laying up a more ample supply of gold in which to invest our reserves.
Has the international monetary fund played fairly with Canada as a great gold producer?
Gold Mining
The international monetary fund for over a year has been turning a blind eye to the fact that South Africa, the world's greatest gold producer, has been marketing 40 per cent of its monthly production in what the minister called today a premium market; in other words, markets outside the monetary fund- and there are lots of such markets. For let us bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that many countries of the world which are important traders in gold are not members of the international monetary fund, and pay no attention whatsoever to the restrictions imposed by the international monetary fund upon its members. And there are, of course, great free gold markets today in the world. We find some of them in Europe and some of them further east, which pay no attention to the restrictions imposed by the international monetary fund, not even in some countries which are members of the international monetary fund. For instance, France has a very important market for the trading of gold that pays no attention to the restrictions imposed by the international monetary fund.
South Africa gold mines have been selling in the free or "premium" market 4-8 million ounces of gold in a year; in other words, 20 per cent more than Canada's total gold production. South Africa has been selling that quantity in what the Minister of Finance called the "premium" market. Canada faced with that situation, I submit, Mr. Speaker, just cannot sit back and watch her interests being dissipated while South Africa enjoys that very substantial advantage-and substantial advantage it is, sir.
If you will look at our own government publication called Foreign Trade for May, 1951, at page 839 you will find an article entitled "Gold-mining industry essential to economy of South Africa" written by the Canadian government trade commissioner to that country. In that article you will find this paragraph:
As in the case of other gold producing countries. South Africa is keenly interested in the prospect of a higher official price for gold, in fact she is the chief promoter of such an increase. A growing percentage of her production, in the form of processed and semi-processed metal, is being sold on the free market. This percentage today is put at over 40. The price in the opening days of 1951 reached $44.50 per ounce in Europe and about $35 in the Far East.
Then, further down:
Sales of other minerals by South Africa last year broke all records, according to statistics recently published by the Mines Department.
There you see South Africa pursuing her interest in this matter and enjoying a substantial advantage because of the fact that she markets 40 per cent of her monthly gold

Gold Mining
production outside the restrictions imposed by the international monetary fund.
Now, sir, what was Canada's position? What was the position that the Canadian cjelegate to the international monetary fund took when this question of freeing the shackles on South Africa came before that fund for consideration and when the fund decided apparently to permit South Africa to take this large percentage of its gold production outside the confines of the international monetary fund? I would like to hear the Minister of Finance tell the house just what was the position taken by the Canadian delegation on that question at the meeting of the governors of the fund. Did Canada acquiesce? Was Canada silent? Did Canada put forward any plea for similar treatment on her own behalf? Well, if she did not, Mr. Speaker, I say that this government failed to discharge an important duty that it owed to the gold mining industry, a very leading foundation for Canada's whole economy.
Sir, my time is passing quickly. I wish to conclude by indicating what I think are the courses of action open to Canada in a realistic appreciation of this situation, and due appreciation of where Canada's interest lies. The first course would be through the international monetary fund. That will necessitate effective demand on the part of the Canadian government for revision of the policy of that fund, and a demand for treatment similar to that received by South Africa. If the United States resists in order to avoid what it might consider to be domestic inflationary pressures, then I think we must have regard for Canadian interests and no longer submit this important gold industry to the sacrifices that it has been called upon to make.
The governors of the fund meet next September, and unless out of that September meeting comes a drastic revision of the policy of the fund as it affects the marketing of Canadian gold and the price for Canadian gold, this parliament will have to face up to the necessity of giving serious consideration to withdrawing from the fund. I would not wish to see a withdrawal from the fund without one last supreme effort being made to bring about in the interests of Canada a drastic revision in the policy of the fund. Therefore I say that this September meeting must represent Canada's offer of a last opportunity to the fund. If the fund is not prepared to proceed with due regard for Canada's interest, then Canada will have to face a serious alternative.
Of course, that alternative is to fall back on the free market, which means selling gold

in any form in Canada or elsewhere. There are a number of free markets in certain areas in the world today. A big free market exists in Portugal, there is a market in the east and so on. Of course United States policy with reference to the purchase of gold can have an important effect upon the future of the free market. That is why I should like to see something done, if possible, through the agency of the international monetary fund in the way I have indicated. If they will not proceed to revise their policy in the light of Canadian interests then I think we will just have to accept the situation and sell our gold in the available markets.
Here is evidence of a recent sale by La Luz mine in Nicaragua at $41.50 per ounce in the free market for all gold produced in the six months ended March 31, 1951.
I must bring these remarks to a close, but in doing so I wish to support a program offered by the Northern Miner in its issue of May 3, which reads:
Our proposition is: Give the citizens and corporations of Canada the right and opportunity
to buy gold
to hold or sell gold
to export gold
in suitable form, of certified fineness, at open market prices, openly arrived at.
Harking back to their December issue, they urge the government to:
1.	Instruct the Department of Finance to remove all discouragement to the purchase, holding, or sale of refined gold by Canadians.
2.	Instruct the Royal Canadian Mint to sell refined gold, in suitable and certified form, and at current open market prices, to Canadians for safekeeping.
3.	Endeavour at the international monetary fund, and through other channels, to persuade the fund and other nations to recognize the traditional usefulness of gold as a medium in which people of all countries can hold some of their individual savings in a form to protect themselves against inflation and currency depreciation, and
4.	Endeavour to persuade the fund and other nations to recognize this private market for gold as worthy of consideration in establishing or revising the price of gold rather than, as at present, imposing harsh controls, even in wealthy North American countries, in order to contain this demand and maintain the market at the monetary price set by the United States dollar parity established in 1934.
Also it was recommended:
1.	That Canadian gold mines be allowed at least as much liberty in exporting gold to non-monetary markets as South Africa, the largest gold producer and member of the fund, has provided to her producers, or
2.	If the Canadian government feels it must restrict exports as the fund requests, then let it pay to producers required to sell at the price established by the fund, a compensation payment equal to the difference between t?his price, and the current price ruling in the non-monetary market from which producers are barred by the action of the fund.
The gold mining industry does not ask for any handout; it does not want to be a burden

on the Canadian taxpayer. Take the shackles off, and give it its freedom, and it will take its chances with world conditions.

I know that the committee is very anxious to get this bill through tonight, and because of that fact I will make my remarks very brief. However, I should not like to allow the hon. member for Kootenay West to get home entirely free with some of the remarks he made earlier this evening. It was a typical C.C.F. statement of policy. I gathered he was speaking for his party, and it was typical of the usual woolly thinking that comes from them. Like Don Quixote he certainly rode his horse madly in all directions, and he succeeded very well. He was for a subsidy and yet he opposed it in principle. That is a very good way of getting money. You allow somebody else to take the responsibility but you still like to get the money. It almost seemed to me that he was

Gold Mining
making a bid lor what they tell me is quite a substantial Social Credit vote in Kootenay West.
However, one thing that was very plain was that he made it abundantly clear that his policy and mine are diametrically opposed, and that certainly gives me great satisfaction. I am now more convinced than ever that there must be something in the policy that I was intending to suggest that is pretty nearly right. As I said, Mr. Chairman, it is getting late, and I know there is hardly time for one more long speech on goldmining assistance. There is only one thing I should like to say. A number of members have emphasized very much-and I think it is a point well taken-the job we are doing to try to assist the gold mines. I think it is working out to be somewhat of a disservice to them'. I think we are encouraging the gold mines as we do a man swimming out from shore. We are trying to get them farther out and into more trouble. It is like feeding somebody ground glass. We are taking advantage of our gold mines. Necessarily they are having to pick out their high grade ore. What I am afraid of is that the time will come when mines, which under ordinary and normal circumstances would be producing gold mines, will have picked out all their high grade ore, and they will not have an economic operation any more.
It has been suggested that I am not sympathetic to the gold mines. My family has been associated with the gold-mining industry of Canada for the last fifty years, and I certainly appreciate very much the tremendous impetus they give to our country in times of deflation. I thank it is unfortunate that the government is doing things in such a niggardly way. Under the policy that we are following now I think we are doing a disservice to these mines that have to pick out their high grade ores in order to keep in operation. I feel that we cannot afford the manpower, certainly in the base metal mines of Canada. We are very short of miners, and if certain marginal gold mines closed down now it would not be too great a hardship.
With respect to the $10 million that the government intends to use for the production of gold, I suggest that the government might use some of that money to assist mines that are forced to close down to maintain their properties in good condition. I say that because to me it is tragic that we are taking this permanent asset, gold, and selling at below cost of production. The time will come in Canada when we will need that gold badly to bolster our economy. That is only a thought for the government. I am certain that the government is not too proud of their

present policy. I think, Mr. Chairman, you will remember what happened when it was first introduced. It came about through the fact that we lost a by-election in Pontiac at a time when the government did not feel they could afford to lose a by-election, and I think they whisked this policy up out of thin air. It is getting very late, and I see that the Minister of Public Works is very much concerned, so I am going to let him get off the hook.

To reply to what the hon.
member for Comox-Alberni has said, he expressed what a lot of shareholders of the gold mining companies have themselves been saying. I have here the report of McIntyre Porcupine Mines Limited, and as it has been published I do not mind giving these figures. The shareholders were asked three questions. The first one was:
Are you in favour of Canada's gold mines being given free access to the world markets for gold, at home and abroad?
The reply was yes, 1,278; no, 20; and undecided, 12. These are interesting questions. The second question was:
Should we, in order to give support to our employees and the mining communities in general, continue to struggle against almost impossible odds until our resources are exhausted?
The reply was yes, 130; no, 1,042; and undecided, 138. The third question was:
Should we, in order to conserve our valuable ore assets, give consideration to suspension of operations until we can reopen the gold mines under more favourable conditions?
The answer was yes, 988; no, 176; and undecided, 146. I want to put that on the record because there is a tremendous body of information among shareholders that this unequal struggle against an impossible formula should be ended. I do so as a warning to the government. It is only because this company, like many others, realize that they have a responsibility to the Dominion of Canada, to the community in which the mine is situated and to their employees that the decision to continue operations is made. I know personally a great many gold mines which would be much better off if they were closed down, and it is only because of their feeling of national duty that they continue to operate.
